title: Inspection Robot Dog: What a Patrol Round Actually Tests
excerpt: A patrol robot is judged by the report it leaves behind, not by the route it walked. What to test before a quadruped earns a night round.
seoTitle: Inspection Robot Dog
metaDescription: What an inspection robot dog is tested on: repeatable waypoints, floor transitions, the sensor payload, and the report a supervisor reads.

faq.q: Can a robot dog replace night security?
faq.a: It replaces the walking of the round, not the judgement. Most sites run it as a sensor carrier that produces evidence, with a person reviewing the report and responding to anomalies.

faq.q: What matters more: legs or sensors?
faq.a: Sensors. The payload decides what the report can contain, which is the only thing the site actually uses the next morning.

faq.q: How do we test one before buying?
faq.a: Five nights at the same waypoint, comparing the images side by side, plus one real report from an operating site. Repeatability first, agility second.

content:
An inspection round looks simple until you watch one run at night. The robot has to find the same door, stop at the same panel, hold a steady angle for the same photograph, and produce something a supervisor can read the next morning. Most of the difficulty is in that last part, and almost none of it is about legs.

THE TEST IN ONE LINE

A patrol robot is judged by the report it leaves behind, not by the route it walked.

A round is a sequence of fixed positions, not a wander

What a site actually deploys is a list: waypoint one is the plant room door at 2100, waypoint two is the switchboard at 2135, waypoint three is the loading dock at 2210. The robot repeats that list every night, at the same angle, in the same light, and the value comes from the repetition. A machine that arrives at the right place from a slightly different direction produces a photograph nobody can compare to last week's.

So the first thing to test is not agility. It is repeatability: five nights, the same waypoint, and a comparison of the five images. If they differ, the platform is not ready for inspection work regardless of how well it handles stairs.

Four things the round actually tests

Floor transitions. Carpet to tile, tile to a ramp, ramp to a dock plate. Each seam is where a quadruped stumbles or re-plans, and each one costs time on a round that has to finish before the morning shift arrives.

Door and threshold handling. A closed fire door stops the round. Either the site integrates access control, or the round is designed around it. Both are decisions, and neither is made by the robot.

The sensor payload. A visible-light camera answers "is the door open". A thermal sensor answers "is that panel hot". An acoustic sensor answers "is that pump running louder than last week". The payload decides what the report can contain, so it is the specification that matters most — more than payload capacity in kilograms.

The output. Every platform claims a report. Ask to see one from a real site, with real timestamps and a real anomaly in it. If the vendor cannot produce a sample report, the software is a demo.

Where the price difference actually comes from

Quadrupeds span a wide range for a reason that is easy to see once you look at the two ends of it. An education unit at the entry level teaches gait, control and programming with an open SDK and a body that a student can repair. An industrial inspection unit carries the payload, the ingress protection and the runtime that a cold storage aisle and a plant room demand — and costs several times as much for capabilities that only matter at night, outdoors, in dust, over a two-hour round.

What changesEducation unitIndustrial inspection unit
Round lengthShort demonstrationsTwo hours, dock to dock, unattended
EnvironmentLab floor, hallwaysDust, ramps, loading docks, weather
PayloadCamera and a laptop linkThermal, acoustic, gas, additional compute
Failure costA lessonA missed round and an unreviewed site
SupportDocumentationSpares, service response, replacement body

The failure that matters most

Not falling over. Missing a round quietly.

A robot that stops in the middle of a building is an inconvenience. A robot that walks the round but fails to capture one waypoint, then files a report that looks complete, is a safety problem: the site believes it was inspected. Ask how the platform handles a partial round — whether it names the waypoints it missed, and whether a supervisor sees that clearly.

A single missed waypoint reported honestly is worth more than a hundred images nobody reviews.

What to check before a pilot

  • Five nights at the same waypoint, images compared side by side
  • A sample report from an operating site, anomalies included
  • How a partial round is recorded and who is told
  • Runtime measured with the real payload, not the brochure number
  • Ingress protection matched to where the round actually goes
  • Which parts a site technician can replace, and which need return to base

The two ends of the range in our catalogue

The MagicLab MagicDog Y1 is the industrial unit: inspection and patrol, payload and runtime for a working night round. The MagicLab MagicDog is the education unit, and it is the right buy for a school or a lab that wants to teach control and gait. Buying the second for a security round is the most common mistake we see; buying the first for a classroom is the second most common.

For teaching and research budgets the AGIBOT D1 EDU sits between them, and it is where most university courses should start.

Send us the route, the waypoints and what the report has to prove. We will tell you whether a quadruped is the right machine for it at all.

title: Humanoid Robot for University Labs: What to Buy First
excerpt: A demo unit performs. A research platform gets opened, reprogrammed and published from. What a university lab should ask before it signs.
seoTitle: Humanoid Robot University
metaDescription: What a university lab checks before buying a humanoid: SDK access, serviceability, spares, safety, and the integration time nobody budgets.

faq.q: Do we need a full-size humanoid for student projects?
faq.a: Usually not. A compact platform such as the AGIBOT X2 Ultra covers most student work on interaction and prototyping; full-size bodies matter when the study is about human presence, scale or balance.

faq.q: What should we ask for before the quote?
faq.a: The SDK reference and a sample repository. A platform whose API documentation arrives after payment is a demonstration device, not a research tool.

faq.q: Who maintains it after the grant ends?
faq.a: Name that person before purchase. Battery ageing, finger wear and firmware updates continue whether or not the project does.

content:
A university buys a humanoid once every few years, and the decision outlives the person who made it. The question that matters is not which machine looks best in a video. It is which machine still has a working SDK, a spare part and a research student on it in two years' time.

THE DIFFERENCE IN ONE LINE

A demo unit performs. A research platform gets opened, reprogrammed, dropped, repaired and published from. Buy the second one.

Start with what you will measure, not with the model

Every lab that regrets a purchase made the same first move: it compared robots. The useful first move is to write down the study. Bipedal locomotion and balance work needs torque transparency and joint control at a low level. Manipulation work needs hands with enough degrees of freedom to hold a real object and enough force feedback to know when it is holding one. Human-robot interaction work needs a face, a voice, and a body that behaves predictably around people who have never seen a robot before.

Those three labs need three different machines. None of them is best served by the model with the best trade-show footage.

What the numbers on the page actually tell you

Degrees of freedom is the number most often quoted and the least often understood. It tells you the shape of the body, not the quality of the control you get over it.

PlatformWhat the spec saysWhat it implies for a lab
LimX LUNA 160 cm, 27 degrees of freedom, AI task editor, video-to-motion, kinesthetic teaching Fast to a working demonstration. Strong for interaction studies, public trials and teaching showcases; the motion tooling is the point, not the joint count.
LimX OLI 33 degrees of freedom, NVIDIA Orin NX at 157 TOPS, ROS2 The research default in this range. ROS2 support means a student can publish to it in the first week rather than the first semester.
ADAM PRO 41 degrees of freedom, modular actuators, integrated motion capture, five-finger hands Aimed at AI labs and industrial work; the modular actuator design matters when something fails at 4pm on a Friday.
Fourier GR-3 55 degrees of freedom, 12 of them in the hands, emotion engine, micro-expression recognition Care and companionship research. Buy it when the study is about people's response to the body, not about locomotion.
AGIBOT X2 Ultra Compact embodied AI platform for prototyping and research The entry point. Smaller body, smaller experiments, much smaller commitment.

Four things that decide whether it survives a semester

None of these appear on a brochure, and each of them has ended a project.

1. SDK access and documentation. Ask for the SDK documentation before the quote, not after. If the vendor cannot send a link to the API reference, the machine is a demonstration device with a robot-shaped body.

2. Serviceability. Ask which parts are field-replaceable and which need to go back to the factory. A humanoid that has to fly to Shenzhen for a knee replacement is unusable in a teaching timetable.

3. Spare parts and consumables. Batteries age whether or not the robot runs. Hands wear at the fingers. Ask what a battery costs and how long it is stocked.

4. Safety behaviour around untrained people. A lab is full of people who will walk in front of a moving robot. Emergency stop placement, force sensing, fall mitigation and speed limits are not optional features when students are the test subjects.

Budget the integration, not the machine

The purchase order is the smallest line in a humanoid project. The larger lines are the research assistant who learns the stack, the replacement parts across three years, the safety assessment for the building, and the time between delivery and the first publishable result.

That last number is the honest one. Ask a vendor what a typical lab reaches a first working demonstration in, and treat a vague answer as an answer.

If the first experiment needs a firmware update nobody at the vendor will send, the platform was never a platform.

What a lab should ask before signing

  • SDK documentation and a sample repository, sent before the quote
  • Which joints and sensors are field-replaceable, and the lead time on each
  • Battery cost and stock life
  • Emergency stop behaviour, force limits and fall handling, in writing
  • The name of another lab running the same model, and permission to call them
  • What the vendor does on delivery day: unboxing only, or commissioning on site

How we choose between them

We ask what the lab intends to publish, what the building allows, and who will maintain it. Then we map the answer to a platform and say plainly when a cheaper machine does the job, or when the honest recommendation is to wait a year.

Two platforms cover most of what we are asked for: the LimX OLI for locomotion and ROS2 research, and the LimX LUNA where the study involves people watching or interacting. For care research the Fourier GR-3 is the different machine it claims to be, and worth the step up only if the research question is about response rather than motion.

Tell us the study, the building and the person who will maintain the robot. We will tell you which platform survives it, and which does not.

title: Humanoid Robot Examples: What Each One Is Actually For
excerpt: A roll call of humanoids is useless on its own. The humanoids we sell, grouped by the work their body suits, and the one number that decides each one.
seoTitle: Humanoid Robot Examples: What Each One Is For
metaDescription: The humanoids we sell and the spec that decides each one's job: joint count, hand type, height, runtime and onboard compute, dated November 2026.

faq.q: Which humanoid robot is best for research?
faq.a: It depends on the experiment. Locomotion and control work points at the LimX OLI, 31 active body joints with a 157 TOPS Orin NX and a complete URDF. Manipulation with real objects points at the PNDbotics ADAM SP, 41 degrees of freedom with five-finger hands. Demonstration-driven work points at the ADAM U, which ships with a motion-capture suit and hands its motion straight to the robot.

faq.q: Is a half-size humanoid still useful?
faq.a: Yes, when the job is interaction rather than handling. The AGIBOT X2 Ultra is 1.31 m and 39 kg, which makes it safe to run in a showroom and easy to transport. The limit is payload: 3 kg is quoted in a specified posture, and full-range payload is no more than 1 kg, so it develops and demonstrates far better than it carries.

faq.q: What is the difference between the ADAM U and the ADAM SP?
faq.a: The SP is the bigger platform: 1.67 m, 62 kg, 41 degrees of freedom, roughly 340 N·m at knee and hip. The ADAM U is a 31-DOF teaching and research machine whose height adjusts from 1.35 m to 1.77 m, sold with a Noitom motion-capture suit and INSPIRE hands. The U is for learning from people; the SP is for doing the work afterwards.

faq.q: Why do sources disagree about humanoid specifications?
faq.a: Because a joint count depends on what you count, and a speed depends on how you measure it. The AGIBOT A3 Ultra is listed at 1.8 m/s by one reseller and 18 km/h by another. The CASBOT 02 is listed at 25 degrees of freedom by one database and 37 in social posts. Ask the vendor to reconcile the numbers in writing, and plan from the lower one.

faq.q: Can a humanoid robot do cleaning work?
faq.a: Not the ones here. A biped that picks things up is not a floor machine, and a scrubber cleans a floor faster with a published area rate. If the job is floor care, buy a scrubber such as the Gausium Phantàs or the Keenon C40-P1. A humanoid belongs where the work is manipulation, inspection or interaction, and even then it repeats taught motions rather than deciding.

content:
Search for humanoid robot examples and you get the same machines in the same order, a spec table underneath, and no statement of what any of them is for. That is the wrong way round. The body decides the job: legs or wheels, fingers or a gripper, one hour of battery or eight, and who can service it when a joint starts to knock.

What follows is the machines we actually sell, grouped by the work their body suits. Prices and specifications are dated November 2026 and carry the kind of evidence behind them: manufacturer specification, independent listing, or our own published offer. Where two sources disagree, the disagreement stays in the sentence instead of being averaged away.

Read the body, not the brochure A 1.31 m machine with a 1 kg working payload and a 1.74 m machine with 5 kg per arm are not competitors. They answer different questions.

Six questions that sort the field

Ask these before you look at a single photograph.

  • What does it stand on? Legs buy stairs and thresholds, and cost runtime plus a fall risk. Wheels buy hours and stability, and stop at a step.
  • What does it hold? A one-joint gripper and a six-joint five-finger hand are different instruments, not trim levels.
  • How tall is it? Reach, sight lines and the space you must keep clear all follow height.
  • How long does one pack last, and in which mode? A runtime without its workload is a marketing number.
  • What does it compute on board? An Orin NX at 157 TOPS runs vision on the robot. A machine without onboard inference needs a PC beside it, and a person to look after the PC.
  • Who services it? A modular actuator a site technician can swap is a different ownership cost from a sealed joint that flies back to the factory.

Research bipeds: the LimX OLI and the ADAM SP

The LimX OLI is the machine a lab buys when the experiment is about walking. LimX publishes 31 active body joints: six per leg, seven per arm, three in the waist, two in the neck (LimX OLI specification, manufacturer data). The 33-DOF figure on our own page is those 31 plus the two one-joint grippers fitted as standard — editorial arithmetic, 31 + 2. Each arm carries 3 kg, with LimX's own caveat that capacity changes with pose and extension.

Two numbers decide whether the OLI fits a project. Perception runs on an NVIDIA Orin NX rated at 157 TOPS, so vision work sits on the robot rather than beside it. The pack is a 9,500 mAh slide-out rated at about 1.5 hours on the specification sheet, with about two hours in the FAQ from laboratory testing. Recorded as a conflict, and the article plans on 1.5. A three-hour block is two to three packs, and every swap is a seated procedure with the robot powered down.

The PNDbotics ADAM SP answers the manipulation question instead: 41 degrees of freedom, five-finger hands, 62 kg, a 1,172 Wh pack, roughly 340 N·m at knee and hip and about 60 N·m at the arm (PNDbotics wiki, manufacturer data). One limit belongs in the brief before an interaction study is written — on the SP the head is listed for display, with articulated neck joints appearing on the Pro model. If the paper needs gaze, specify the Pro in writing.

Imitation learning: the ADAM U turns a person into a dataset

Most humanoids are sold as a body. The ADAM U is sold as a body plus a way of teaching it. It carries 31 degrees of freedom, including a two-joint head, six-joint hands and a three-joint waist with a braking system, binocular vision, and a height that adjusts from 1.35 m to 1.77 m — one machine can run a study with adults and another with smaller participants.

PNDbotics pairs it with Noitom's PNLink motion-capture suit and INSPIRE's RH56E2 six-joint hand, on 25 quasi-direct-drive actuators peaking at 360 N·m (independent report, PNDbotics claims attributed). That combination is what makes the ADAM U the example to name when the method is demonstration: a person moves, the suit records, the robot repeats it. Where it is the wrong purchase: terrain. The gait is built for controlled floors, and an adjustable-height body with a braked waist is not a stair-climbing testbed.

Half-size, full audience: the AGIBOT X2 Ultra

The X2 Ultra is 1.31 m and 39 kg with 30 degrees of freedom, 120 N·m peak joint torque, 1.8 m/s walking speed and a 500 Wh pack good for about two hours (independent reseller comparison of manufacturer figures). Its purpose is the room with people in it: retail floors, showrooms, reception, and prototyping where a full-size machine is too much robot and too much risk.

The payload line is the one buyers skim. Three kilograms is quoted in a specified posture; full-range payload is no more than 1 kg excluding the end effector. A demo that lifts a box proves the joint works. A handling plan has to survive the 1 kg figure, and many do not. Onboard compute is the Ultra's real advantage over the base X2, an Orin NX with 16 GB, because that is the model you can actually develop on.

Full-size performance: the AGIBOT A3 Ultra

The A3 Ultra is the other end of the same idea: 1.74 m, 60 kg, 51 active degrees of freedom, 5 kg per arm, a 1,152 Wh pack and up to eight hours, with peaks around 320 N·m and NVIDIA Thor for onboard inference (reseller listing of manufacturer figures). It is the machine people film. AgiBot's own demonstrations include somersaults and aerial kicks, and our product page repeats that as a demonstration note, not a duty cycle.

Speed is where the sources part company. One listing gives 1.8 m/s; our motion note and one independent database cite 18 km/h, which is 5 m/s. Recorded as a conflict: read the high figure as a sprint inside a demonstration and plan walking speeds from the lower one. What the acrobatics prove is control authority — the machine can absorb a landing — and that is worth something on a public floor. What they do not prove is uptime, and none of the sources behind this piece publishes a failure rate.

Care is a different design: the Fourier GR-3

The GR-3 is the one machine here whose body is shaped by contact rather than by tasks. Fifty-five degrees of freedom, twelve of them in each hand when the dexterous hands are fitted, 165 cm, about 71 kg, and a soft shell carrying 31 pressure sensors (independent listing). Runtime is roughly three hours across two hot-swappable packs, so a swap is a design feature rather than an interruption.

Fourier frames it as care and companionship, and the emotion layer in the head is aimed at the person standing in front of it. That makes the GR-3 the right platform for interaction studies and supervised care pilots, and the wrong purchase for anyone reading "care robot" as a staffing answer. A care deployment needs a risk assessment, insurance, consent and staff acceptance before a spec sheet matters. Its walking speed is reported as 5 or 6.1 km/h depending on the source — another conflict, and one that does not change the decision.

The companion end: Moya and Xiaoling

Not every example is a full body. The DroidUp Moya is a biomimetic companion built for expression, with a human-like gait around 0.83 m/s. It is sold for companion and exhibition work, and its price is listed as coming soon, so it cannot be a budget line yet. Unknown, and stated as unknown rather than guessed.

The Tangible Future Xiaoling 3.0 goes further in the same direction: a head, an expressive face, no legs, and a published wholesale price of USD 5,000 as of November 2026. Our motion library says plainly that no clip fits a head-only rig, which is the honest version of the claim. Its job is reception, teaching and exhibition interaction where the face is the whole point and mobility would only add risk.

Also on the shelf, briefly

Three more bodies answer narrower questions. The CASBOT 02 EDU is a full-size biped aimed at university teaching and interaction research; one independent database lists 25 degrees of freedom while social posts about the same platform claim 37, a conflict to put to the vendor before a specification is written. The Kepler S-PE BumbleBee is a 30-DOF, 75 kg industrial biped with 100 TOPS of onboard compute, built for uneven ground and push recovery rather than performance. The MagicLab MagicBot G1 is the general-purpose full-size platform, joints around 350 N·m, for teams that want one machine to attempt several jobs.

What the body is forMachineThe number that decides it
Locomotion and control researchLimX OLI31 body joints; 1.5 h on a 9,500 mAh pack
Manipulation researchPNDbotics ADAM SP41 DoF; five-finger hands; 340 N·m knee
Imitation learningPNDbotics ADAM U1.35–1.77 m adjustable height; mocap suit
Prototyping and retail interactionAGIBOT X2 Ultra1 kg full-range payload
Public-facing performanceAGIBOT A3 Ultra51 DoF; 5 kg per arm; up to 8 h
Care and interaction studiesFourier GR-355 DoF; 31 touch sensors; ~3 h
Companion and exhibitionDroidUp Moya0.83 m/s gait; price unpublished
Reception interaction onlyXiaoling 3.0Head only; no motion-library clip fits

What none of them do

None of these machines does unscripted work. They walk, they gesture, some of them grasp, and every one of them is better at repeating a taught motion than at deciding what to do next. A humanoid bought as an answer to a labour problem usually arrives as a project instead: a route to define, a charging place to build, a person assigned to start it, and a spare parts budget nobody wrote down.

None of them cleans a floor. If the job is floor care, a scrubber does it in a third of the time with a published area rate — the Gausium Phantàs and the Keenon C40-P1 exist for that, and a biped that picks things up is not a substitute.

Every machine here is made to order and lands in 8 to 12 weeks, imported from China with a 12-month warranty, and the warranty excludes wear parts and consumables on the platforms whose terms are published. Spare-module prices and lead times are not published anywhere I could read, so that is a conversation to have with the supplier before the purchase order, not after the first fault.

What to do next

Write the job on one page before you compare machines: the room, the task, the object, the hours, and the person who will stand beside it. Then match the body. Research on walking and control points at the LimX OLI, published at USD 65,900 wholesale as of November 2026. Dexterous manipulation points at the ADAM SP at USD 89,000. Interaction studies with people in the room point at the GR-3 at USD 188,000, or at a head like the Xiaoling 3.0 at USD 5,000 if a face is all the job needs.

Whichever you shortlist, ask for four things in writing: the URDF and SDK documentation, the maintenance schedule and who is allowed to run it, the lead time for a replacement joint or hand, and the name of the person who answers at 2am. A humanoid that cannot be serviced on site is an exhibition, however good the film.

Tell us the room and the task. We will tell you which body fits it, which one does not, and what it takes to keep it running.

title: Humanoid Robot Jobs: Roles That Appear After Deployment
excerpt: A humanoid creates four roles: operator, maintainer, data steward and safety lead. Sites that skip naming them switch the robot off.
seoTitle: Humanoid Robot Jobs
metaDescription: A humanoid creates four roles: operator, maintainer, data steward and safety lead. Name them before the machine arrives.

faq.q: Who operates a humanoid day to day?
faq.a: Usually an existing team member with an added duty. The failure mode is nobody being formally responsible.

faq.q: What does a data steward do?
faq.a: Decides what the robot records, how long it is kept, who can see it, and what happens when a camera captures a customer.

faq.q: Why train two people?
faq.a: Because one trained operator means the robot idles whenever that person is on leave.

content:
A humanoid does not arrive and start working. It arrives and creates work: operators, maintainers, data handlers and a safety role that did not exist in the job description last year.

THE SHIFT

Automation moves jobs from doing to supervising, and supervision is a skill that has to be trained rather than assumed.

The operator

Someone has to start the round, watch the first ten minutes, respond when the machine stops, and decide whether the stop is a fault or a floor hazard. In practice this is an existing team member with an added duty, and the failure mode is that nobody is formally responsible for it.

The maintainer

Batteries age, joints wear, sensors drift out of calibration. A humanoid fleet needs someone who can read a fault log, replace a module and know when to escalate. On single-unit sites this is usually a technician with training from the vendor; on multi-site deployments it becomes a role.

The data steward

Robots produce logs, images and sensor streams. Someone has to decide what is kept, for how long, who can see it, and what happens when a camera records a customer. That is a governance job, and it lands on whoever owns privacy in the organisation.

The safety lead

A full-size machine moving near people needs a documented operating envelope, a risk assessment and a stop procedure. Regulators increasingly expect a named person behind that document, and internal auditors ask for it before insurers do.

RoleAppears whenUsually filled by
OperatorDay oneExisting front-line staff with added duty
MaintainerFirst fault, or month threeFacilities technician, vendor-trained
Data stewardBefore the first camera goes livePrivacy or IT owner
Safety leadBefore the first public deploymentOperations manager or WHS officer

What to do before the robot arrives

  • Name the operator in writing, with the duty in their role description
  • Book vendor training for at least two people, not one
  • Decide the data retention rule before the first recording
  • Write the stop procedure and rehearse it once
  • Agree who is called at 3am, and what they are allowed to do

For sites building that capability ahead of deployment, education platforms such as CASBOT 02 EDU and ADAM U are how a team learns the stack before the operational machine lands.

Ask who does each of those four jobs on your site. If the answer is nobody, that is the finding.

title: Humanoid Robot Price: What Moves the Number
excerpt: A humanoid quote is a set of engineering decisions with a number attached: degrees of freedom, hands, battery, sensors and support.
seoTitle: Humanoid Robot Price
metaDescription: What moves a humanoid quote: degrees of freedom, dexterous hands, battery sizing, sensor payload and the support tier.

faq.q: What is the largest cost step after the body?
faq.a: Dexterous hands with force control. A gripper picks up a box; a hand picks up a cup.

faq.q: Does more degrees of freedom always cost more?
faq.a: Yes — every joint is an actuator, a controller and calibration time, and more joints mean more to maintain.

faq.q: How do I compare two quotes honestly?
faq.a: Compare commissioning, training, spare parts stock, response time and warranty exclusions, not just the headline figure.

content:
A humanoid quote is not a price. It is a set of engineering decisions with a number attached, and understanding the decisions is the only way to compare two quotes honestly.

WHAT MOVES THE NUMBER

Degrees of freedom, hands, battery, sensors, and what the vendor promises after delivery.

Degrees of freedom, and where they are

Every joint is an actuator, a controller and a calibration. A 27-degree performance robot and a 55-degree care robot are not in the same cost class because of what the extra joints do, not because one is better built.

Ask which joints exist. Arms and legs are the visible ones; hands are where the price climbs fastest, because a five-finger hand with force control costs more than several limbs.

Hands decide the work

A gripper can pick up a box. A dexterous hand can pick up a cup. If the research or the deployment needs the second, the hand specification drives the quote more than the body does.

Battery, and the cost of running

A battery pack sized for continuous operation costs more than one sized for a demonstration, and it ages regardless of use. Ask the replacement interval and the cost of the pack, because it recurs.

What the vendor promises after delivery

Commissioning on site, training, spare parts stock, response time and warranty exclusions are all priced somewhere. A quote that is lower and silent on those four points is not lower; it is incomplete.

DecisionEffect on the quote
Degrees of freedomMore joints, more actuators, more calibration time
Dexterous handsThe single largest step in cost after the body
Battery and runtimeHigher up front, lower per year if sized correctly
Sensor payloadAdds cost and adds weight, which adds actuator cost
Support tierConverts a capital question into an annual one

The three questions that shrink a quote

  • Which joints does the study actually use, and can we buy fewer
  • Does the work need dexterous hands or a gripper
  • What support tier do we genuinely need in year two

We quote ADAM U and AGIBOT X2 Ultra on opposite ends of this ladder, and we will tell you when the cheaper one does the job — which is more often than most quote requests assume.

Send the use case, not the wishlist. The number follows the decisions, and we can name them one by one.

title: Quadruped Robot Dog: Six Models and Who Each One Suits
excerpt: Six quadrupeds, and the honest answer for each is a type of buyer rather than a list of specifications.
seoTitle: Quadruped Robot Dog
metaDescription: Six quadruped models and who each one actually suits: education kits, research units and industrial inspection machines.

faq.q: Which quadruped suits teaching?
faq.a: An education class unit such as MagicDog, AGIBOT D1 EDU or Genisom L1 EDU, chosen for documentation and repairability.

faq.q: Which suits a night patrol?
faq.a: An industrial unit with payload, runtime and ingress protection, such as MagicDog Y1 or Genisom M1.

faq.q: What separates the classes in practice?
faq.a: Payload, runtime, environmental sealing, spares and support — not the leg mechanism itself.

content:
Quadrupeds look alike in a video and differ enormously in a spreadsheet. Six models, and the honest answer for each is a type of buyer rather than a list of specifications.

HOW TO READ THIS

Nobody buys a quadruped for its gait. They buy it for the payload it carries, the ground it crosses, and who has to keep it running.

The education end

The MagicLab MagicDog is the entry point: a small quadruped for teaching, STEM programs and hobbyist work, where the value is an open platform a student can program and repair. The AGIBOT D1 EDU and Genisom L1 EDU occupy the same space with more documentation and a support structure behind them.

Buy this class when the objective is learning. Do not buy it for a security round; it will not carry the sensors or last the night.

The industrial end

The MagicLab MagicDog Y1 is built for inspection and patrol: payload capacity, runtime and a body intended to work outside a lab. The Genisom M1 targets security patrol and site monitoring, with the integration work that implies.

This class is bought by facilities and security teams, and the decisive questions are about support and spares rather than peak performance.

The research middle

Between them sit platforms bought by universities that need a real payload and a real SDK without an industrial support contract. That is where most labs land, and where the specification conversation is longest.

ModelClassBuilt for
MagicLab MagicDogEducationTeaching, STEM, hobbyist projects
AGIBOT D1 EDUEducationCourses and lab work with documentation
Genisom L1 / L1 EDUEducation, researchTeaching and research labs
MagicLab MagicDog Y1IndustrialInspection and patrol rounds
Genisom M1IndustrialSecurity patrol and site monitoring

What separates the classes in practice

  • Payload: a camera versus a camera, thermal and additional compute
  • Runtime: a demonstration versus a two-hour round
  • Ingress protection: a corridor versus a loading dock
  • Support: documentation versus a service response
  • Spares: order by part number, or fabricate

We stock MagicDog Y1 for inspection work and MagicDog for teaching, and we will say when the cheaper one is the honest recommendation.

What the class does not tell you

Within a class, models still differ in ways that only surface in use: how the SDK is documented, whether the battery is swappable, how the machine behaves on a wet ramp, and whether the vendor answers a support email in a day or a fortnight.

Ask each vendor for the same three things — a sample API call, a spare parts list, and the name of a customer running the same model — and compare those, not the marketing pages.

Tell us what the robot has to carry and where it has to walk. The class follows from those two answers.

title: Quadruped Robot Kit: Teaching vs Research Buying
excerpt: A quadruped for a classroom and one for a research group diverge in week six, when something breaks and a course is waiting.
seoTitle: Quadruped Robot Kit
metaDescription: Teaching needs repairability and documentation; research needs an SDK and payload. Buying one class for the other is the common mistake.

faq.q: What matters most for a classroom robot?
faq.a: Repairability and documentation, plus parts on the shelf so a fault does not stop a semester.

faq.q: What matters most for research?
faq.a: Payload for the sensors the study needs, an open control interface and logging fast enough for analysis.

faq.q: How many units does a class need?
faq.a: One per class or a shared pool is workable, as long as the exercises are designed around availability.

content:
A quadruped kit bought for a classroom and one bought for a research group look similar in a catalogue and behave completely differently in week six, when something breaks and a course is waiting.

THE DIFFERENCE

Teaching needs repairability and documentation. Research needs an SDK and a payload. Buying one for the other is the most common mistake in this category.

What teaching actually requires

Twenty students, one robot, a timetable. The machine has to survive being handled by people who have never touched one, and it has to be fixable by a technician without a return-to-base shipment in the middle of semester.

Documentation matters more than capability: a course needs exercises that work, an SDK a student can read, and a fault that produces a message rather than a mystery.

What research actually requires

One robot, one question, and a need to record everything. Payload for the sensors the study needs, an open control interface, and the ability to log at a rate that makes analysis possible.

Research groups often buy the education class and then discover the payload mounting and the logging rate are the limiting factors — after the grant has been spent.

RequirementTeachingResearch
RepairabilityEssential: parts on the shelfUseful
DocumentationEssential: exercises and examplesUseful: API reference matters more
PayloadMinimalDecisive
LoggingNice to haveDecisive
QuantityOne per class, or a shared poolOne per project

The questions that decide it

  • How many students will touch it in a semester
  • What has to mount on it, in grams
  • Who repairs it when a leg actuator fails on a Tuesday
  • What the course needs to demonstrate by week twelve
  • Whether the SDK has examples a student can run unassisted

For teaching we point at AGIBOT D1 EDU and the Genisom L1 EDU; for research with a payload, the industrial class is usually cheaper over three years than replacing education units that cannot carry the experiment.

The cost of getting it wrong

Buy an education unit for research and the payload limit shows up in month two, when the sensor mount does not fit and the logging rate is too slow for the analysis. Buy an industrial unit for teaching and the machine sits unused because nobody has time to learn a support contract.

Both mistakes cost a full budget cycle. The cheap correction is a short conversation with the people who will actually use it, before the purchase order.

title: Quadruped Robot Price: Four Decisions That Set It
excerpt: Four decisions set a quadruped's price: payload class, sensor load, ingress protection and support tier. Each one can be declined.
seoTitle: Quadruped Robot Price
metaDescription: Payload class, sensor load, ingress protection and support tier are the four decisions that set a quadruped robot's price.

faq.q: Why do similar quadrupeds differ so much in price?
faq.a: Payload class and environmental sealing change the structure and actuators, not just the options list.

faq.q: Is support tier worth paying for?
faq.a: On a single-unit site it is often the difference between a working robot and an expensive object in a cupboard.

faq.q: When is the cheaper machine right?
faq.a: When the round is a camera along a corridor and a person reviews the images. Not when a thermal finding at 2am is the deliverable.

content:
Two quadrupeds with similar proportions can differ by a factor of eight, and the reasons are specific. None of them is "better robot".

FOUR DECISIONS

Payload class, sensor load, ingress protection, support tier. Each one moves the number, and each one is a choice you can decline.

1. Payload class

A frame that carries a small camera and a frame that carries thermal, acoustic and additional compute are different machines underneath: actuators, structure, thermal design. Payload is the first divider in this category and the one buyers underestimate.

2. Sensor load

The sensors themselves are often a modest part of the cost and a large part of the value. A thermal camera changes what a round can report; it also changes the software that has to ingest the stream. Budget the integration, not just the camera.

3. Ingress protection

An indoor corridor and an outdoor loading dock are different environments. Sealing against dust and water costs engineering, and it is not a feature you can add later with a cover.

4. Support tier

The gap between "documentation" and "a response within a working day, with spares on the shelf" is a real part of the price, and it is the part that decides whether the robot is working in year two. On a single-unit site it is often the difference between a deployed robot and an expensive object in a cupboard.

DecisionCheaper choiceWhat it costs later
Payload classCamera-only frameCannot carry the sensors the round needs
Sensor loadVisible light onlyReports describe, they do not diagnose
Ingress protectionIndoor specFails at the dock, or needs a shelter
Support tierDocumentation onlyWeeks of downtime on a single fault

Where a cheaper machine is the right answer

If the robot carries a camera along a corridor and a person reviews the images, an education-class unit does the job. If the round has to produce a thermal finding at 2am in a plant room, it does not — and buying the cheap one twice is how a project loses a year.

  • Weigh the payload, including mounts and cabling
  • Name the sensors the report has to include
  • Match ingress protection to the worst point on the route, not the average
  • Price the support tier over three years, not one

We quote MagicDog Y1 and Genisom M1 for industrial rounds, and we will say when a cheaper class covers the same route honestly.

Send the route and the report you want at the end of it. That is the specification, and the number follows it.

title: How Much Is a Robot Dog: What Each Step Buys
excerpt: Toy, education, industrial: what each step buys, and how to tell which step you are actually on.
keywords: how much is a robot dog
seoTitle: How Much Is A Robot Dog
metaDescription: What a robot dog buys at each step — toy, education, industrial — and how to tell which step your site is actually on.

faq.q: Is a toy robot dog a small industrial robot?
faq.a: No. It has no meaningful payload, no logging and no support. It is a different product with the same silhouette.

faq.q: What does the education step add?
faq.a: An SDK, documentation and a repairable body — the things that let a person program and fix it.

faq.q: What does the industrial step add?
faq.a: Payload, runtime, ingress protection and a service relationship with response commitments.

content:
The question people ask in a showroom is not the question they should ask, but it is a fair one. The useful answer is not a figure. It is what changes between the cheap end and the working end.

THE STEPS

Toy, education, industrial. Each step buys a capability, not a look.

Step one: the toy

A toy quadruped walks, responds to a remote and impresses a room. It has no meaningful payload, no logging and no support. It is not a small industrial robot; it is a different product with the same silhouette.

Step two: education

An education unit adds an SDK, documentation and repairability — the things that let a person program it and fix it. This is the class where most first purchases should land, because it teaches the buyer what the next purchase needs to do.

Step three: industrial

An industrial unit adds payload, runtime, ingress protection and a support contract. At that point the robot is a tool with an operating cost and a service relationship, and the questions change from "what can it do" to "what happens when it stops".

StepWhat you getWhat you do not
ToyMovement, novelty, remote controlSDK, payload, support
EducationSDK, documentation, repairable bodyWeather sealing, long runtime
IndustrialPayload, runtime, sealing, serviceCheap entry, simple ownership

How to decide which step you are on

  • Is the robot a demonstration or a tool
  • Does anything have to mount on it
  • Does it have to work when nobody is watching
  • Who repairs it, and how long can it be down
  • Will there be a second unit in two years

If the answers point at a tool, the honest conversation is about the industrial class — MagicDog Y1 or Genisom M1. If they point at learning, MagicDog is the right first purchase and a good one.

What a second purchase looks like

Almost nobody buys one quadruped. If the first one earns its keep, a second arrives within two years — often a different class, because the first taught the buyer what the round really needs.

That is worth planning for: choose a vendor and a support arrangement that can scale from one unit to a small fleet, rather than one that treats each robot as a separate relationship.

Buy the step you are on. Buying two steps ahead usually means a machine nobody is trained to run.

title: What Is a Robot Dog: the Capability Line People Miss
excerpt: Mobility is solved; payload, endurance and reporting are not. The capability line people miss when they buy a robot dog.
seoTitle: What Is A Robot Dog
metaDescription: A robot dog is not a dog or a vacuum. The line sits between it can walk over there and it can do something useful when it arrives.

faq.q: Why legs instead of wheels?
faq.a: Legs handle stairs, kerbs, gravel and cable trays. On a smooth corridor a wheeled platform is cheaper and simpler.

faq.q: Does a robot dog replace a person on a round?
faq.a: It replaces the walking and produces a record. It does not decide, open doors or handle a spill.

faq.q: What should I ask first?
faq.a: What it can carry and for how long, what it records and in what format, and what happens when it cannot complete the route.

content:
A robot dog is not a dog and not a vacuum. The capability line people miss sits between "it can walk over there" and "it can do something useful when it arrives".

THE LINE

Mobility is solved. Payload, endurance and reporting are not.

Why legs at all

Wheels are efficient on flat, prepared ground. Legs exist for the places wheels cannot go: stairs, kerbs, gravel, cable trays, the gap between a pallet and a wall. If the route is a smooth corridor, a wheeled platform is cheaper and simpler, and nobody should apologise for choosing it.

What "robot dog" actually describes

A quadruped with a sensor head, a compute payload and a control interface. The leg mechanism is the visible part; the useful part is what hangs off it and what it can record.

That is why two machines that look identical in a photograph can be entirely different products: one carries a camera for a classroom, the other carries thermal and acoustic sensors for a plant room at night.

What it does not do

It does not decide. It does not open doors, climb ladders or handle a spill. It does not replace a person on a round; it replaces the walking of the round and produces a record of it.

ExpectationReality
It patrols the siteIt repeats a mapped route and stops at set points
It spots problemsIt captures what its sensors can see; a person interprets
It works outdoorsOnly models rated for it, and only within their limits
It runs all nightIt runs a round, then charges

The three questions that reveal the real product

  • What can it carry, and for how long at that weight
  • What does it record, and in what format does that land
  • What happens when it cannot complete the route

Answer those three and the category becomes obvious: MagicDog for learning, MagicDog Y1 when the round has to produce evidence.

The maintenance reality

Legs wear. Feet take the impact, joints take the load, and the machine that walks 8 kilometres a night for a year will need attention that a wheeled platform does not. Ask what the service interval is, what a leg assembly costs, and whether a site technician can fit one.

This is not a reason to avoid quadrupeds. It is a reason to price ownership honestly rather than comparing purchase prices only.

If the route is flat and the job is inspection, ask us whether wheels would do it better and cheaper. Sometimes they would.

title: Service Robot: What Actually Runs After the Demo
excerpt: Uptime, spares, consumables and training decide whether a service robot was a good purchase. None are visible in a showroom.
seoTitle: Service Robot
metaDescription: Uptime, spares, consumables and training decide whether a service robot was a good purchase. What to measure in the first quarter.

faq.q: What is the right uptime question?
faq.a: Not will it break, but how long will it be broken and who fixes it. Ask for the response commitment in writing.

faq.q: Which consumables should I price?
faq.a: Brushes, squeegees, filters, wheels and batteries, with replacement intervals, before you sign.

faq.q: Why is the first month not the test?
faq.a: Routines settle because everyone is paying attention. The test is the quarter after, when the robot is just equipment.

content:
Every service robot looks convincing in a demonstration. The question that decides whether it was a good purchase is duller: what happens in week nine, when the novelty is gone and something has stopped working.

WHAT RUNS AFTER THE DEMO

Uptime, spares, consumables and training. Four things, none of them visible in a showroom.

Uptime is the product

A robot that works 90 per cent of the time sounds fine until the missing 10 per cent lands on the busiest night of the week. Ask what the vendor's response commitment is, and what the site is expected to do while waiting.

The honest question is not "will it break" but "how long will it be broken, and who fixes it".

Spares and consumables

Brushes, squeegees, filters, wheels, batteries. Every service robot consumes something, and the consumption rate is the operating cost nobody quotes at the start. Ask for the list and the interval.

Training, and who actually gets it

Sites that train one person end up with one person who can run the robot, and a machine that idles whenever that person is on leave. Train at least two, and put the operating procedure somewhere it can be found by a night shift supervisor who was not in the room.

The first month is not the test

Routines settle in the first month because everyone is paying attention. The test is the quarter after, when the robot is another piece of equipment and the person who championed it has moved on.

What to measureWhy it matters
Rounds completed vs scheduledReveals quiet failure before a complaint does
Mean time to repairDecides whether one fault ruins a week
Consumable spend per monthThe real operating cost
Number of trained operatorsCover for leave and turnover
  • Response time in writing, not in conversation
  • Consumables list with prices and intervals
  • Two trained operators minimum
  • A named person who owns the daily check
  • A first-quarter review with the numbers above

For a single-unit deployment we usually start with the Keenon C40-P1; for lobbies and corridors where the round is simpler, the Gausium Phantas has fewer systems to maintain.

The handover problem

Service robots outlive the person who championed them. When that person leaves, the operating knowledge usually leaves with them unless it was written down: the route, the charging routine, the fault codes, and the name of the person at the vendor who answers.

Write a one-page operating sheet, keep it where the night shift can find it, and review it when anything about the building changes. It is the cheapest uptime improvement available.

Ask any vendor for their mean time to repair before you ask for the price. The answer tells you what ownership looks like.

title: Delivery Robots Australia: Indoor, Outdoor, and the Line
excerpt: Indoor delivery robots integrate with a building. Outdoor robots integrate with a street that is not yours, and that changes everything.
seoTitle: Delivery Robots Australia
metaDescription: Delivery robots in Australia: the dividing line is not indoor versus outdoor, it is whether the machine shares space with the public.

faq.q: What is hardest about an indoor deployment?
faq.a: Lift and door integration, plus a drop-off the guest or patient can use without training.

faq.q: What is hardest about an outdoor deployment?
faq.a: Footpaths, kerbs, weather, public consent, local regulation and insurance — not navigation.

faq.q: Can a pilot prove too much?
faq.a: Yes. A perfect summer pilot says nothing about a wet Tuesday, and a quiet-fortnight pilot says nothing about peak.

content:
Australia is a difficult place for delivery robots and an easy place to be misled about them. The line that matters is not indoor versus outdoor. It is whether the machine has to share space with the public.

THE DIVIDING LINE

Indoors, the building is the environment. Outdoors, the street is — and the street is not yours.

Indoor delivery: the building is the constraint

A hotel, hospital or office tower gives a delivery robot a floor plan, lifts, doors and a predictable population. The hard parts are integration, not navigation: lift control, secure drop-off, and a guest or patient who has never met the machine.

This is where delivery robots work today, and where the ROI conversation is simplest, because the alternative is a person walking a tray across a lobby at 11pm.

Outdoor delivery: the street is the constraint

Footpaths, kerbs, weather, traffic, dogs, and a public that did not agree to any of it. Australian cities are also not uniform: a wide Melbourne footpath and a narrow Sydney one are different operating environments, and a machine rated for one may be unacceptable on the other.

Then there is the regulatory layer, which is local, and the insurance layer, which is yours.

ConsiderationIndoorOutdoor
Environment ownerYou, or the buildingThe public
Biggest integrationLifts and doorsKerbs, crossings, weather
Regulatory burdenLowLocal, variable
InsuranceStandardNeeds explicit cover
Failure visibilityInternalPublic

What to settle before a pilot

  • Who owns the floor the robot drives on, and who insures it
  • Lift integration, or a manual workaround that survives a busy night
  • What happens when a guest refuses to interact with it
  • Whether the route crosses any public land
  • Who is called when it stops in a corridor at peak hour
An indoor pilot can fail quietly. An outdoor pilot fails in front of everyone, which is why the insurance question comes first.

Where the deployment is hospitality or exhibition-facing, the platform conversation usually starts with something like DroidUp Moya. Where the robot is moving through a building to keep it running rather than to greet anyone, the Keenon C40-P1 does the same routing work with a cleaning payload instead.

The pilot that proves too much

A pilot that runs perfectly in summer tells you nothing about a wet Tuesday in July. Where a machine will operate outdoors, run it through the worst week available, not the best one.

Indoors the equivalent is the peak: run the pilot during the busiest period the building has, with the public present, rather than in a quiet fortnight when everyone is on leave.

Tell us whether the route leaves the building. That single answer changes the machine, the insurance and the timeline.

title: Restaurant Service Robot: the Floor Plan Decides
excerpt: A restaurant service robot is decided by aisle width, turning space and whether a plate of soup survives the floor. Measure first.
seoTitle: Restaurant Service Robot
metaDescription: Restaurant service robots are decided by aisle width, turning space and tray stability. Measure the room before choosing the machine.

faq.q: What should I measure first?
faq.a: The narrowest gap between a table and a wall, and the turning space at the end of each run.

faq.q: How do I test tray stability?
faq.a: A demonstration with liquid, at service speed, on your own floor, including any lips between tiles.

faq.q: Who should be asked?
faq.a: The floor team. They know which aisle is already a problem at 7pm on a Friday.

content:
Restaurants buy service robots for the labour they think they will save, then discover the floor plan decides whether the machine is useful. Aisles, turning circles and tray stability are the specification.

THE FLOOR PLAN DECIDES

A robot that cannot pass between two tables at peak service is not a service robot. It is a conversation piece.

Aisle width and turning circles

Measure the tightest gap between a table and a wall, and the space needed to turn at the end of a run. Most restaurants have one aisle that works and two that do not, and the robot will spend its life in the one that does.

Where the floor plan is tight, the platform choice narrows quickly — which is better discovered before purchase than after.

Tray stability is the real test

Carrying a plate is easy. Carrying a bowl of soup across a floor with a 3mm lip between tiles is the test. Ask for a demonstration with liquid, at service speed, on your own floor.

Pickup and delivery windows

A service robot exists to move something from the pass to a table and back. If the kitchen has to change its workflow to load the machine, the labour saving disappears into a new bottleneck at the pass.

ConstraintWhat to measure
Aisle widthNarrowest gap between table and wall
Turning spaceRoom to turn at the end of each run
Floor transitionsTiles, lips, carpet edges, ramps
Pass layoutWhere the machine docks without blocking service
Peak densityGuests and staff moving at the same time

What staff actually think

Ask the floor team, not the owner. They will tell you which aisle is already a problem at 7pm on a Friday, and whether an extra body in that aisle is help or obstruction. That answer is worth more than any demonstration.

  • Measure the aisles at peak, with chairs out
  • Test with liquid, at service speed
  • Walk the pass workflow with the kitchen
  • Ask two servers whether the route helps or blocks
  • Decide who clears a stopped robot during service

Where the room is generous and the job is carrying, a service platform such as DroidUp Moya fits the brief. Where the floor is tight and the need turns out to be cleaning rather than carrying, the compact end of the range — the Gausium Phantas — is the more honest answer.

Send a floor plan with the table layout. We can tell you in five minutes whether a robot fits the room.

title: Hotel Delivery Robot: Lifts, Privacy and the Night Desk
excerpt: Hotels are the natural home of the delivery robot and where they fail most visibly. Lifts, privacy and the night desk decide it.
seoTitle: Hotel Delivery Robot
metaDescription: Hotel delivery robots live or die on lift integration, guest privacy and who is on the night desk when the machine stops.

faq.q: Can a robot use a hotel lift?
faq.a: Only with an interface, or a staff workaround that costs minutes on every trip and erodes the labour saving.

faq.q: What must guests be told?
faq.a: What the robot records, who sees it and what happens to the data. A plain notice at check-in solves most of it.

faq.q: What should a first pilot cover?
faq.a: One floor, one shift, one purpose — and a stop procedure the night desk has rehearsed.

content:
Hotels are the natural home of the delivery robot and the place where they fail most visibly. The reasons are lifts, privacy and the night desk.

THREE INTEGRATIONS

Lift control, door access and guest communication. Each one is a building decision, not a robot decision.

Lifts

A delivery robot that cannot call a lift is a trolley that cannot leave the ground floor. Lift integration is either a supported interface or a manual workaround where a staff member presses a button — and the workaround erodes the labour saving with every trip.

Privacy and the guest

A machine arriving at a door at 10pm with a camera on it raises questions the hotel has to answer before it deploys: what is recorded, who sees it, and what the guest is told. A short, plain notice at check-in solves most of it, and the absence of one creates the complaint.

The night desk

The person on the desk becomes the robot's operator by default. If the machine stops in a corridor at 2am, they are the one who deals with it — and if nobody decided that in advance, it becomes a reason to switch the robot off.

IntegrationWhat it needsWho owns it
LiftsInterface or a staff workaroundBuilding systems
Room doorsAccess method for drop-offFront office and security
Guest noticePlain-language disclosureOperations
Night escalationA named person and a procedureDuty manager

What a hotel should pilot

  • One floor, one shift, one purpose — toothbrushes and towels, not room service
  • Lift integration confirmed, or the workaround costed in staff minutes
  • Guest notice written and approved
  • Night desk given a stop procedure they have rehearsed
  • A weekly review of trips completed versus trips attempted

For hospitality deployments the platform conversation usually starts with something like DroidUp Moya. Where the hotel's real problem is floors rather than deliveries, the Keenon C40-P1 addresses a larger share of the night.

What guests actually notice

Guests do not mind a robot in a corridor. They mind a robot that blocks the corridor, arrives at the wrong door, or makes a noise outside their room at 10.40pm.

That makes the schedule a hospitality decision rather than a technical one: which floors, which hours, and what the machine does when a request is urgent and a lift is busy.

Start with one floor and one purpose. The lift integration is the project, not the robot.

title: Service Robots Examples: Six Deployments That Hold Up
excerpt: Six service robot deployments that survive a real building, and the habit each one depends on to keep working.
seoTitle: Service Robots Examples
metaDescription: Six service robot deployments that hold up in real buildings: cleaning, patrol, research, retail, demonstration and lab support.

faq.q: Which deployment is most reliable?
faq.a: Night cleaning in a hotel or office: regular floors, an empty building and one person checking the result.

faq.q: Why do deployments quietly fail?
faq.a: Because nobody reads the output each morning, so the floor degrades and the machine is blamed.

faq.q: Which deployment is easiest to cost?
faq.a: Lab and manufacturing support: controlled environment, repeatable task, measurable output.

content:
Six deployments that survive contact with a real building, and what each one is actually good at. None of them is a demo.

WHAT MAKES A DEPLOYMENT HOLD

A regular environment, a clear owner, and a job the machine can finish without a person standing next to it.

1. Night cleaning in a hotel or office

The classic case, and still the strongest: a mapped route on regular floors, run when the building is empty, checked each morning by one person. Coverage is the deliverable and the map does the work.

2. Perimeter and plant-room patrol

A quadruped carrying a camera and thermal sensor along a fixed route, producing a report a supervisor reads at 7am. The value is the record, not the walking.

3. Research and teaching

A humanoid platform in a lab, where the deployment is measured in papers and student projects rather than hours saved. This one holds because the output is knowledge, and knowledge does not care about ROI.

4. Retail floor maintenance during trading hours

Cleaning while the public walks around it. This works best where the route is wide and the machine is quiet, and it fails in narrow formats where staff and shoppers compete for the same aisle.

5. Public-facing demonstration

A performance humanoid in a mall or exhibition. The deliverable is attention, and the deployment is judged on whether it ran all day without an incident — which is a real engineering test even when the purpose is marketing.

6. Laboratory and manufacturing support

Wheeled humanoid platforms moving material or holding position in a controlled environment. Less glamorous, more repeatable, and the easiest case to cost honestly.

DeploymentMachine classWhy it holds
Night cleaningCleaning robotRegular floor, empty building, one checker
Patrol roundQuadrupedFixed route, report output
ResearchHumanoid platformOutput is knowledge
Retail during tradeCleaning robotWide routes, quiet operation
Public demonstrationPerformance humanoidAttention is the product
Lab supportWheeled humanoidControlled environment, repeatable task

We stock across these classes — Gausium Phantas for cleaning rounds, MagicDog Y1 for patrol — which means the recommendation is about the building rather than the catalogue.

The deployment that quietly fails

The one nobody complains about. The robot runs, the report is filed, and nobody reads it — so a floor degrades slowly and the machine is blamed when the client finally notices.

Every deployment on this list depends on one human habit: somebody opening the output each morning and acting on it. Without that, the machine is producing evidence for an audience of nobody.

Tell us which of the six looks like your building. The other five are probably a distraction.

title: How to Buy a Commercial Robot in Australia: the Sequence

seoTitle: How To Buy Commercial Robot Australia
metaDescription: The sequence for buying a commercial robot in Australia: brief, site survey, trial, commercial terms, commissioning and review.

faq.q: What should the brief contain?
faq.a: One page: what the machine must do, where, who runs it, and what result counts as success. Not a feature wishlist.

content:
Buying a commercial robot in Australia is a sequence, and the failures happen when the steps arrive out of order: a quote before a site survey, a trial after a decision, a support arrangement nobody wrote down.

THE SEQUENCE

Brief, site survey, trial, commercial terms, commissioning, review. Skip one and the project pays for it later.

1. The brief

One page: what the machine has to do, where it has to do it, who will run it, and what result counts as success. Not a wishlist of features. Sites that write this page make every later conversation shorter.

2. The site survey

Walk the building with the vendor. Aisles, thresholds, charging position, floor transitions, network coverage, and the loading route for delivery. Survey findings change the shortlist more often than the shortlist changes the survey.

3. The trial

A trial that runs the actual round, at the actual hour, for at least a week. Anything shorter measures enthusiasm rather than fit.

4. Commercial terms

Purchase, hire or staged deployment. What is included, what is a consumable, what the support tier covers, and what happens at the end of the warranty.

5. Commissioning

Mapping, route design, training for at least two people, and a documented operating procedure. This is where the deployment becomes real.

6. The review

Thirty days after go-live: rounds completed, faults, consumable spend, and whether the hours freed were used as intended. The review is the step everyone skips and the one that decides whether a second unit follows.

StepOutputWho signs off
BriefOne page of requirementsOperations
Site surveyRoute and constraints mapVendor and facilities
TrialMeasured performance on the real routeOperations
TermsWritten inclusions and exclusionsFinance
CommissioningMapped route, trained operatorsVendor and site lead
ReviewNumbers, not impressionsOperations

What buyers in Australia should ask specifically

  • Who provides service, and from where
  • Spare parts stock held locally, or shipped per order
  • Lead time, which is often the real constraint on a programme
  • Whether the vendor commissions on site or ships a box
  • What the warranty excludes

We run that sequence on every deployment, including the parts where the answer is that a robot is not the right purchase. It is the same path for a Gausium Phantas as for a Keenon C40-P1.
