title: Robot Hire Australia: When Renting Beats Owning
excerpt: Hiring a robot is a different instrument, not a discount. Short demand, an unproven site, or capital that has somewhere better to go.
seoTitle: Robot Hire Australia
metaDescription: When hiring a robot beats buying one: seasonal demand, an unproven route, or capital timing. What the hire agreement must say.

faq.q: When is hire the better choice?
faq.a: Seasonal peaks, an unproven site, or a capital delay. Buy when the round is stable and long term.

faq.q: Does hire avoid the setup work?
faq.a: No. A hire still needs a survey, a mapped route, trained operators and a charging position.

faq.q: What must the agreement cover?
faq.a: Maintenance responsibility, damage versus wear, consumables, exit condition and what happens if the site does not suit the machine.

content:
Hiring a robot is not a discount version of buying one. It is a different financial instrument for a different problem, and it is usually right in three situations.

WHEN HIRE WINS

Short demand, an unproven site, or capital that has somewhere better to go.

Seasonal and short-term demand

A venue with a three-month peak, an event, a temporary facility: the machine is needed hard and then not at all. Hiring turns a depreciating asset into an operating cost that ends with the season.

The unproven site

When nobody is sure the round works — the floor is irregular, the night window is short, the team is sceptical — hire is the honest way to find out. Six weeks of hire buys evidence that a purchase decision otherwise guesses at.

Capital timing

Sometimes the site is ready and the capital is not. A hire period can bridge a financial year without delaying the operational change, and the decision about ownership can be made later with better information.

SituationHireBuy
Seasonal peakYesOnly if the peak repeats annually for years
Unproven routeYes: it is a trial with a costOnly after evidence
Capital constrainedPossible bridgeWhen cash allows
Long-term steady stateExpensive over yearsYes
Multi-site rolloutRarelyYes, after one site proves the model

What a hire agreement must say

  • Who maintains the machine during the hire, and how fast
  • What counts as damage versus wear
  • Whether consumables are included
  • What happens if the site turns out not to suit the machine
  • The exit date and the condition it has to be returned in

The test of whether hire was right

At the end of the period, can you answer whether the round works, with numbers? If yes, the hire did its job whether or not you buy. If no, the period was a rental, not a decision.

We arrange both paths for the machines we stock, including the Gausium Phantas and the Keenon C40-P1, and we will say when a hire is the better commercial answer.

What hire does not solve

It does not remove the site work. A hire still needs a survey, a mapped route, trained operators and a charging position. Some sites expect the short commitment to mean a lighter setup, discover the same commissioning effort, and conclude the machine was not worth it.

The setup is the project whether the term is six weeks or six years.

Tell us the period and the uncertainty. Hire is a decision tool before it is a financial one.

title: Autonomous Mobile Robots: the Vocabulary Buyers Get Wrong
excerpt: AGV, AMR, cobot, humanoid: four terms used as one. The vocabulary determines the quote, and most specifications get it wrong.
seoTitle: Autonomous Mobile Robots
metaDescription: AGV follows a path, AMR decides a path, a cobot shares a workspace, a humanoid is shaped like a person. Why the words matter.

faq.q: What is the difference between an AGV and an AMR?
faq.a: An AGV follows a fixed path. An AMR builds a map and reroutes, so it survives a layout change.

faq.q: Is a cobot mobile?
faq.a: Usually not. A cobot is an arm working at a station, designed to share space with a person.

faq.q: Why does the vocabulary change the price?
faq.a: Because vendors quote what the specification describes. Mixing classes produces quotes that are not comparable.

content:
Autonomous mobile robot, AGV, cobot, humanoid. Four terms used interchangeably in procurement documents and meaning four different things. The confusion costs money at the specification stage.

THE SHORT VERSION

AGV follows a path. AMR decides a path. A cobot shares a workspace with a person. A humanoid is shaped like one.

AGV: automated guided vehicle

Follows a fixed route — tape, wire, markers, or a defined lane. Extremely reliable, extremely inflexible. Change the layout and the installation changes with it. Still the right answer in high-throughput, fixed-flow environments.

AMR: autonomous mobile robot

Builds a map and navigates it, rerouting around obstacles. The difference from an AGV is not intelligence for its own sake; it is that the installation survives a layout change. This is the class most warehouses and hospitals are actually buying.

Cobot: collaborative robot

An arm designed to work alongside a person, usually with force limits and safety-rated monitoring. A cobot does not move through a building; it works at a station. Mixing the term up with AMR leads to specifications that ask for both mobility and manipulation from one purchase.

Humanoid: a body, not a capability

A humanoid describes a shape. It may walk, it may roll. What it can do depends on its hands and its software, which is why two humanoids can be entirely different products.

TermWhat movesTypical job
AGVAlong a fixed pathRepetitive transport, fixed flow
AMRAnywhere on a mapTransport in changing layouts
CobotAn arm, at a stationAssembly, inspection, machine tending
HumanoidA biped or wheeled bodyManipulation, interaction, research

Why the vocabulary matters commercially

  • A specification that says "autonomous" but describes a fixed route will be quoted twice
  • Asking for manipulation and mobility in one unit narrows the market sharply
  • Safety cases differ by class, and the class is determined by how it moves
  • Support models differ: a fleet of AGVs and one humanoid are not the same service relationship

Most of what we sell is in the AMR and humanoid classes; UniX AI Panther and MagicLab MagicBot G1 show the range between them.

How the vocabulary reaches the quote

Vendors quote what the specification asks for. A document that mixes classes will produce quotes that are not comparable, and the cheapest will usually be the one that quietly answered a narrower question.

Write the movement, the payload and the environment in plain words. Let the vendor attach the acronym, and check that every quote describes the same job.

Write the job, not the acronym. The acronym is where specifications go wrong.

title: Warehouse Robot Cleaner: Dust, Pallet Gaps, Night Windows
excerpt: A warehouse floor is not a lobby with pallets. Dust load, pallet gaps and a short night window change the machine and the round.
seoTitle: Warehouse Robot Cleaner
metaDescription: Warehouses need sweeping before scrubbing, plan for pallet gaps and racking, and work inside a quiet window shorter than expected.

faq.q: Why is sweeping usually first?
faq.a: Cardboard dust, wrap and strapping dominate. A combination unit sweeps, scrubs, vacuums and dries in one pass.

faq.q: Who cleans under racking and between pallets?
faq.a: A person. The robot covers open aisle, and that division should be planned rather than discovered.

faq.q: What decides the machine in a warehouse?
faq.a: The quiet window and aisle width before floor area, plus filtration if dust is the main problem.

content:
A warehouse floor is not a lobby with pallets on it. Dust loads, pallet gaps, forklift traffic and a night window that is shorter than anyone planned make it a different cleaning problem.

WHAT CHANGES

Debris type, floor condition, and when the machine is allowed to be there.

Dust and debris are the primary load

Warehouses produce cardboard dust, shrink wrap, strapping, grit from tyres and whatever the yard brings in. That is a sweeping problem before it is a scrubbing problem, which is why combination machines dominate this category.

Pallet gaps and racking legs

A robot cleans the open aisle. It does not clean under racking, between pallets, or around the legs where debris accumulates. Plan for a person with a blower or a walk-behind in those zones, and do not count that time as a failure of the machine.

The night window

Warehouses often run 24 hours with a short quiet period. That window is the machine's entire opportunity, and it determines runtime and charging strategy more than floor area does.

Warehouse conditionWhat it demands
Cardboard dust and wrapSweeping first, then scrubbing
Pallet gaps and rackingHuman detail work alongside the robot
Forklift trafficObstacle handling and clear operating rules
Short quiet windowRuntime and opportunity charging
Concrete slabScrubbing with the right pad, and dust control

What to settle with the operations team first

  • The quiet window, agreed with shift supervisors rather than assumed
  • Forklift exclusion zones and how they are enforced
  • Who clears debris the machine cannot reach
  • Charging position that does not block a traffic lane
  • What the report has to show for a manager to trust it

For warehouse floors we usually quote the Keenon C40-P1, whose four-in-one pass matches the debris mix. Where the floor is clean and the issue is dust film rather than debris, the Gausium Phantas does the job with fewer systems to maintain.

Air quality is part of floor cleaning

In a warehouse, sweeping lifts dust that then settles on racking and stock. A machine with poor filtration moves the problem rather than solving it, and the dust returns within the shift.

Ask about filtration and about where the exhaust goes. It is rarely in the brochure and it is the difference between a cleaner floor and a dustier one.

Send the window and the aisle width. Those two decide the machine before floor area does.

title: Inspection Robot Price: Sensors Set the Number
excerpt: An inspection robot's cost is mostly its sensors: visible light describes, thermal diagnoses, acoustic and gas predict.
seoTitle: Inspection Robot Price
metaDescription: An inspection robot's price is mostly its sensors. Visible light describes, thermal diagnoses, acoustic and gas predict.

faq.q: Which sensor should come first?
faq.a: Visible light. It answers whether something looks different, at the lowest cost and with the least integration work.

faq.q: What does thermal require beyond the camera?
faq.a: A stable position, a consistent angle and a baseline to compare against — a process requirement, not just hardware.

faq.q: How do I keep sensor costs honest?
faq.a: Start from the finding you need at 7am, then work backwards. Ask what the integration costs, not just the camera.

content:
An inspection robot's price is mostly its sensors. The body, the legs and the software matter, but the number moves with what the machine can see.

SENSORS SET THE NUMBER

Visible light describes. Thermal diagnoses. Acoustic predicts. Each layer changes what the report can claim.

Visible light: description

A camera records what a person would have seen. It answers "is the door open", "is there a spill", "did something fall". It is the cheapest layer and the one every platform has.

Thermal: diagnosis

A thermal camera answers a different question: is this panel hotter than it was last week. That requires a stable camera position, a consistent angle and a comparison against a baseline — which is a software and process requirement as much as a hardware one.

Acoustic and gas: prediction

Sound and gas sensors move the round from inspection to early warning. They also add integration work: capturing the stream, aligning it in time, and setting thresholds that do not cry wolf.

SensorWhat the report can sayWhat it adds
Visible lightSomething looks differentBaseline cost, minimal integration
ThermalThis asset is running hotCamera, calibration, baseline process
AcousticThis machine sounds differentCapture, thresholds, false-positive tuning
GasSomething is present in the airCertification, alarm logic

How to keep the number honest

  • Start with the finding you want at 7am, then work backwards to the sensor
  • Ask what the integration costs, not just the camera
  • Require a sample report from a live site with a real anomaly
  • Check whether the sensor data is exportable for your own analysis
  • Decide who tunes thresholds so the alarms stay credible
A thermal camera on a robot that stands in a different place each night produces noise. Repeatability is what turns a sensor into evidence.

For a first round the MagicDog Y1 with a camera payload will answer most facility questions. Add sensing when the question requires it, not because the brochure lists it — and if the site is a fixed security post rather than a moving route, a patrol platform such as the Genisom M1 is the cheaper shape of the same answer.

The question before the sensor list

What decision will this report change? If the answer is "we would send someone to look", a camera payload is enough. If the answer is "we would shut down an asset", the sensor and the baseline process both have to be right, and the cost sits in the process rather than the hardware.

Start with the decision. The sensor list writes itself after that.

Name the finding you need. The sensor list and the number follow from it.

title: Commercial Cleaning Robots Australia: The First 30 Days
excerpt: The first month of a cleaning robot is not about the machine. It is route measurement, the gap between rated and real coverage, the water round, and the inspection that decides clean.
seoTitle: Commercial Cleaning Robots Australia: First 30 Days
metaDescription: What month one of a commercial cleaning robot really looks like: measured routes, rated versus real coverage, the water round and who signs off clean.

faq.q: How long before a cleaning robot runs a full night on its own?
faq.a: Most sites reach an unattended night round inside four weeks. Week one is mapping and supervised passes, week two is working out the refill rhythm, and by week four the machine repeats a route while one person checks the result. If the route has doors, lifts or a tap two floors away, add a week for each.

faq.q: Does a cleaning robot replace a cleaner?
faq.a: It replaces the walking, not the judgement. Edges, corners, spills, carpet and the inspection at the end stay with people, because those are decisions rather than coverage. On most sites the night team ends up smaller by the hours spent pushing a scrubber and unchanged everywhere else.

faq.q: What breaks first on a new cleaning robot site?
faq.a: The building, not the robot. A fire door that was supposed to be propped open, a charger fitted behind a locked store room, a lift that needs a code, or a network blackspot in the basement. Every one of those is cheaper to fix in the site survey than in the first month.

content:
A cleaning robot does not arrive working. It arrives on a pallet with a charger, a manual and a commissioning appointment, and the first month decides whether it becomes part of the night round or a machine parked in the store room behind the mop sink.

This is the sequence Australian sites actually go through: what has to be true before the first run, what the rated numbers mean once a floor is involved, and the four weeks in which a building either absorbs the machine or quietly rejects it.

The short version Measure the route before you choose the machine. Plan the scrub round on the practical coverage figure, not the rated one. Expect the water round, not the robot, to be the real constraint in week two.

What has to be true before the first night

Two numbers decide whether a floor robot can work your route at all, and neither of them is on a brochure. The first is the narrowest clear width on the route. Both machines we import need 650 mm of clear passage: the Gausium Phantàs and the Keenon C40-P1 are rated to the same minimum in their manufacturers' specifications (Gausium specifications; Keenon C40 datasheet).

The second is the charger. It needs power, a clear approach and a position that does not sit behind a locked door at eleven at night. On more sites than not, the only spare power point is in a corridor the night team cleans last, which puts the machine at the far end of the building exactly when it wants to recharge.

For scale: the Phantàs measures 585 × 445 × 619 mm and weighs 65 kg. The C40-P1 measures 616 × 550 × 690 mm with its squeegee fitted and weighs 70 kg with the battery. Both will pass a standard Australian lift lobby. Neither will pass a fire door with a door closer set tight against the wall, so walk the route with a tape measure before anything is ordered.

The rated number is not the number you will see

Gausium publishes two coverage figures for the Phantàs, and the gap between them is the most useful thing on the page. Theoretical scrubbing coverage is 1,188 m²/h at a 330 mm scrubbing width. The manufacturer's own practical figure is 350–700 m²/h. The TASKI-branded datasheet for the same machine, sold into the contract-cleaning channel, goes lower again: a maximum productivity of 700 m²/h and a realistic productivity of 200–400 m²/h (TASKI Phantas technical data).

The difference is turns, doorways, furniture, foot traffic and refills. Rated coverage assumes a clean straight run. Real coverage is what you get in a corridor with a trolley parked in it at 2am. Plan the night on the practical figure and the machine finishes. Plan it on the rated figure and the morning shift finds half a floor done.

A number that does not agree Our own product page quotes 15 hours of continuous runtime for the Keenon C40-P1. Keenon's current page says up to 12 hours sweeping and up to 5 hours scrubbing. Treat the 15-hour figure as an optimistic sweep number at best. Plan the scrub round on five hours, and ask for the runtime in writing for the mode you intend to run.

The C40-P1 is the wider machine: 400 mm scrubbing and vacuuming width, 560 mm sweeping with the side brushes, a 16 L clean tank against 11 L of waste, and a published cleaning efficiency of up to 1,100 m²/h. The Phantàs is the one that gets into tighter space: 465 mm sweeping width, 11.5 L clean and 10.5 L waste, and a six-litre dust bag the manufacturer says holds three to seven days of dust depending on the site.

For reference, the pages publish wholesale dealer prices of USD 9,250 for the Phantàs and USD 10,700 for the C40-P1 as of November 2026, both made to order on an 8–12 week lead time with a 12-month standard warranty, on-site setup and training, and Tier 1–2 support. Those are dealer prices, not landed prices — ask for the delivered figure for your postcode.

Week one is mapping, and it is not automatic

Both machines navigate by SLAM (simultaneous localisation and mapping) and build their map by driving the floor. The first run is supervised, slow and boring, and it is the most valuable half hour of the whole month, because everything afterwards — coverage, the route that gets skipped, the report nobody reads — is decided there.

What the map gets wrong, it gets wrong in the same three places every time: glass walls and mirrors, where the laser passes through or bounces; polished stone under a hard downlight, where the reflection reads as an obstacle; and anything parked where the map was recorded, which becomes a phantom obstacle once it moves. Walk behind the machine on the first pass and correct the map by hand rather than letting it relearn a fault for a month.

Week two is the water round

This is the week that surprises facilities managers. A scrubber is a wet process, and the tank sizes set the rhythm of the night. Eleven and a half litres of clean water on the Phantàs and 16 L on the C40-P1 sound generous until you calculate the refills for a 6,000 m² floor.

Do not calculate it from the tank volume. Count it. In the trial, ask the operator to log every refill and every dump for two nights, note the distance to the nearest tap and drain, and multiply by the wage of the person doing the walking. If the tap is two floors away, the water round can consume the saving the robot was bought for. A machine that docks to a water station solves this; a machine that docks only to a charger does not.

Week three is where the human work shows up

Once the middle of the floor is reliably clean, the complaints change address. They move to edges, lift lobbies, the three square metres around the coffee machine and the corners behind the bins — the places a machine with a 330 mm or 400 mm deck cannot reach. That is not a failure. It is the honest shape of the work, and it is worth showing the client: a floor that is 85 per cent machine-cleaned and 15 per cent hand-finished is a different contract from one that is 100 per cent hand-cleaned, and it should be priced and staffed as such.

Two limits are worth stating out loud before anyone is disappointed. Neither machine is a carpet extractor, so carpeted areas stay with people or separate equipment. And neither replaces the judgement call at 3am about whether a spill needs a second pass — somebody still has to look.

Week four is the inspection

By the fourth week the machine is repeating a route unattended and the question becomes who signs off that the floor is clean. Agree the test before the robot arrives: which zones, at what time, checked by whom, under what light. Coverage reports from the app are evidence of where the machine went, not of how the floor looks. The two are related and they are not the same thing.

What breaks that is not the robot

  • A door that closes. The route assumed a fire door propped open at 11pm. It is not propped open, and the machine waits politely all night.
  • A lift that needs a code. Multi-floor cleaning lives or dies on lift integration, and integration is a building project, not a robot feature.
  • A charger in the wrong place. Cheapest problem on this list to fix before delivery, most expensive to fix after.
  • Nobody trained to read the error screen. Both machines stop for reasons they print on a screen. If only one person on the roster can read it, the machine stops for the week that person is on leave.
  • A network blackspot. Fleet reporting and remote support both need the machine online, and basements are basements.

The second machine on the same shift

Most Australian sites that buy a floor robot in 2026 are also looking at something else for the same night window — a patrol quadruped for after-hours security, or a delivery robot for the hotel floors. It is worth planning the two together, because they compete for the same three things: the lift, the wireless network and the one supervisor on shift.

If a patrol machine such as the MagicLab MagicDog Y1 is walking the same corridors, agree the route order so neither spends the night waiting behind the other. If a delivery robot such as the Droidup MOYA is using the same lift, decide which machine owns the lift schedule between midnight and four. Two robots with one supervisor is a staffing decision before it is a technology decision.

What to ask for before you sign

Ask for a written 30-day commissioning plan: the site survey with measured clear widths, the mapping session with a named person on site, the refill count from a trial on your own floor at the hour it will actually run, the runtime for the mode you will use, and the name of the person who answers the phone when the machine stops at 2am.

Then run one night. One night on your floor, with your team, at your hour, tells you more than any demonstration in a showroom. Both machines are available to trial through us: the Gausium Phantàs for tight routes and smaller floors, and the Keenon C40-P1 where one machine has to sweep and scrub the same concourse.

Send us the floor plan and the hours the building is empty. We will tell you which machine fits the route, what the first month looks like on your site, and what to measure before anything is ordered.

title: Floor Scrubber Robot: Which Machine Fits Which Floor Type
excerpt: Scrubber, sweeper or four-in-one: floor type, deck width and tank size decide which cleaning robot a building needs. The narrowest doorway usually decides it first.
seoTitle: Floor Scrubber Robot: Which Machine Fits Your Floor
metaDescription: How floor type, deck width and tank size decide which cleaning robot a building needs, and where a four-in-one machine stops being the right answer.

faq.q: Do I need a scrubber or a sweeper?
faq.a: A scrubber if the floor is wet-washable and the soil is film, grease or tyre marks. A sweeper if the debris is dry and the floor should not get wet, such as a warehouse slab or a loading dock. A four-in-one machine if both are true on the same floor in the same night.

faq.q: Does deck width really matter?
faq.a: It decides whether the machine reaches the floor at all. The Gausium Phantàs scrubs at 330 mm and the Keenon C40-P1 at 400 mm, and both need 650 mm of clear passage. Measure the narrowest doorway on the route before you compare coverage figures.

faq.q: Can one machine clean carpet and hard floor?
faq.a: A four-in-one can vacuum short-pile carpet and scrub hard floor in the same shift, but it is not a carpet extractor. Deep soil in carpet stays with people or separate equipment. Treat the carpet capability as maintenance cleaning, not as a replacement for extraction.

content:
A scrubber and a sweeper do different jobs, and buildings buy the wrong one because the bigger machine looks more capable. The question is not which robot is best. It is what is on your floor at the hour the machine runs.

Three things decide it: whether the floor tolerates water, how wide the machine has to be to cover the route, and how much water or dust it can carry before somebody has to walk to a tap.

The choice in one line Scrub when the floor is wet-washable and soiled with film. Sweep when the debris is dry and the floor cannot take water. Buy the four-in-one only when both are true on the same night.

What each machine actually does

Scrubbers lay solution, agitate it and vacuum it back up. They lift film, tyre marks and grease off sealed hard floors: tile, vinyl, polished concrete, stone. They need water, a drain, and a floor that tolerates moisture for the minutes before the squeegee passes.

Sweepers pick up dry debris with brushes and suction. They suit warehouses, car parks and loading docks where dust, packaging and grit are the problem and water would be a hazard.

Four-in-one machines do all of it in one pass. Both machines we import work this way: sweep, scrub, vacuum and dry, with the dry waste separated from the wet so the dust box does not turn into mud. That separation is the reason one machine can run a mixed site — and the reason maintenance takes longer at the end of the shift.

Two widths decide the round

Width is where the specification sheet and the building disagree. The Gausium Phantàs scrubs and dust-mops at 330 mm and sweeps and vacuums at 465 mm. The Keenon C40-P1 scrubs at 400 mm and sweeps at 560 mm with its side brushes fitted. A wider deck covers more floor per pass and fits through fewer doorways.

Both machines are rated to a minimum clear passage of 650 mm. If your narrowest doorway, service corridor or toilet block entrance is under that, neither machine gets in, whatever the coverage figure says. Measure first, choose second.

Tanks decide the night

The Phantàs carries 11.5 L of clean water and 10.5 L of waste, plus a six-litre dust bag that Gausium says holds three to seven days of dust. The C40-P1 carries 16 L clean and 11 L waste with an eight-litre dust bag. Bigger tanks mean fewer walks to the tap, and the distance to the tap is what actually costs money in a night round.

Runtime follows the same logic, and it is where the numbers need reading carefully. Gausium publishes the Phantàs at 4.5 hours scrubbing, 4.5 hours vacuuming, 6 hours sweeping and 10 hours dust-mopping, with roughly two hours to charge. Keenon publishes the C40-P1 at up to 5 hours scrubbing and up to 12 hours sweeping. Those are mode-specific maxima under test conditions, not a shift length.

Watch the mode The sweeping runtime is the number that gets quoted, and it is usually two to three times the scrubbing runtime. If you intend to scrub, plan on the scrubbing figure — or on a battery swap. The C40-P1 is built for a five-second battery change, which is a different answer to the same problem.

Floor types, and where each machine fails

FloorWorksFails because
Polished concreteScrubber or four-in-oneDust film returns within a day once the squeegee blade wears
Vinyl and safety flooringScrubber at low solution flowWater sits in the texture and dries streaky
Short-pile carpetMachine vacuum on a carpet-rated model; the C40-P1 auto-detects carpetNeither machine is an extractor, so deep soil stays with people
Warehouse slab with pallet gapsSweeper or four-in-oneDebris collects in the gaps the brush cannot reach
Stone and terrazzoScrubber with the right padThe wrong pad dulls the finish and nobody notices for a month
Polished floor under hard downlightsBoth, with careReflection confuses optical navigation; expect map corrections

Wet floors and everything else on them

A scrubbed floor is wet for a couple of minutes, sometimes longer in a humid lobby, and that matters for anything else running on the same floor. A delivery robot such as the Droidup MOYA sharing a hotel corridor cannot tell a wet patch from a dry one, and neither can a guest. Keenon quotes around 30 seconds of drying after the squeegee on the C40-P1; treat that as the manufacturer's figure for a clean pass on a level floor and give the corridor a margin before the next machine or the first guest uses it.

The practical fix is scheduling, not technology. Scrub the through-routes first and let them dry while the machine works the side areas, so the wet window never overlaps the busiest ten minutes of the building's evening.

What to test on your own floor

  • The narrowest doorway on the route, measured with a tape, not estimated
  • One full pass on the dirtiest floor at the hour the machine will actually run
  • Where it fills and empties, and the walking time to a tap and a drain
  • Whether the floor dries before anyone walks on it, timed with a stopwatch
  • Who cleans the machine at the end of the shift, and how long that takes
  • What the floor looks like in the morning, judged by the person who complains about it

For reference, the pages publish wholesale dealer prices of USD 9,250 for the Phantàs and USD 10,700 for the C40-P1 as of November 2026, both made to order on 8–12 weeks. Both figures are dealer prices, so ask for the landed number for your site.

What we would put on your floor

Send us the floor plan and the hours the building is empty, and we will tell you whether you need a scrubber, a sweeper or a four-in-one, then name the machine. For tight routes, service corridors and floors under about a thousand square metres, the answer is usually the Gausium Phantàs: 330 mm scrub path, 650 mm minimum passage, and a quiet mode at or below 60 dB for hospitals and hotels that run it near guests.

For a concourse or a mall where one machine has to sweep and scrub the same floor in the same night, the answer is usually the Keenon C40-P1: 400 mm scrub path, 560 mm sweep, 16 L of clean water, and a battery you can swap in five seconds instead of waiting two hours for a charge.

Two questions decide it: what is on the floor, and how narrow is the narrowest gap on the way there. Send both and we will answer with a machine and a configuration.

title: Are Cleaning Robots Worth It: Three Tests Before You Buy
excerpt: Three tests decide whether a cleaning robot earns its place: how much of the night is walking, how regular the floor is, and who checks the result at seven.
seoTitle: Are Cleaning Robots Worth It? Three Tests to Run First
metaDescription: Practical coverage is 350-700 m2/h, not the rated figure. Three tests decide whether a cleaning robot earns its place on your site.

faq.q: How much floor can one charge clean?
faq.a: The Gausium Phantàs scrubs for 4.5 hours on a charge. At TASKI's realistic 200–400 m²/h that is 900–1,800 m²; at Gausium's practical 350–700 m²/h it is 1,575–3,150 m². Plan the first month on the low number and let the trial move it up.

faq.q: Do I need staff on site overnight to run it?
faq.a: Not to drive it, but somebody has to refill water, empty waste and clear a fault. Both machines return to the charger by themselves and neither clears a jam, so a site with nobody in the building overnight needs a fault plan before it needs a robot.

faq.q: Does a cleaning robot replace a cleaner?
faq.a: It replaces the walking of the round, not the judgement. Edges, door reveals, bathrooms, spills and the morning inspection stay with people. On most sites the machine takes the regular floor area and the crew keeps the irregular work, which is why the roster rarely shrinks by a full shift.

faq.q: What usually goes wrong first?
faq.a: Nobody owns the morning check. The machine reports coverage, the report is not read, a streak appears in the lobby, and within a month the crew has stopped trusting it. Naming one person who inspects the floor at seven prevents more failures than any specification change.

content:
Worth is not a property of the robot. Two buildings can buy the same machine and one gets a clean floor every night while the other parks it behind the mop sink by the second week. What separates them is the round.

Three tests decide it, and all three can be run before any money moves: how much of the night is walking, how regular the floor is, and whether anyone will look at the result at seven in the morning.

Three tests, in order Is the floor regular? Is the round unsupervised? Does anyone check the result? Two yes answers earn a trial. One yes means the machine gets parked, and the reason will be written off as the robot.

Test one: how much of the night is walking

A manufacturer publishes two coverage figures, and the gap between them is the most useful number on the sheet. Gausium rates the Phantàs at 1,188 m²/h theoretical scrubbing at a 330 mm scrubbing width, then states a practical range of 350–700 m²/h alongside it (Gausium specifications, manufacturer specification, checked November 2026). The theoretical number assumes a clean straight run with no doors, no turns and nobody in the way.

TASKI, which sells the same machine into the contract-cleaning channel, is blunter: 700 m²/h maximum and 200–400 m²/h realistic, for spaces up to 1,000 m² (TASKI technical data, independent channel datasheet, 2024). The Keenon C40-P1 is rated up to 1,100 m²/h at a 400 mm scrub width (Keenon product page, manufacturer specification, checked November 2026).

The arithmetic that decides the shift is per charge, not per hour. The Phantàs scrubs for 4.5 hours on a charge. Multiply that by the practical rates and one charge covers 900–1,800 m² on TASKI's conservative figure, or 1,575–3,150 m² on Gausium's — a calculation, not a quoted specification, and worth doing on the low number first (editorial inference from manufacturer figures). The C40-P1 scrubs for up to 5 hours, which raises the ceiling, but only while the water in the tank is still doing its job.

So count your scrub-able floor before you compare machines. A night round of 1,200 m² of lobby and corridor is one charge with margin. A 6,000 m² round across four levels is not a robot purchase at all; it is a small fleet with chargers, spares and a refill routine, and it should be designed that way from the start.

Test two: is the floor regular

Regular means the machine can drive most of the area in long passes: corridors, concourses, open retail, lobby stone. Irregular means door frames, columns, plinths, toilet cubicles, stair landings and the strip behind a counter.

Both machines need 650 mm of clear passage and both are roughly the size of a loaded cleaning trolley. The Phantàs measures 585 × 445 × 619 mm; the C40-P1 measures 616 × 550 × 690 mm with its squeegee fitted. A fire door with the closer set tight against the wall is narrower than the doorway says, and a housekeeping cart parked in a corridor turns a 1,200 mm passage into a 400 mm one at exactly the hour the machine runs.

Level changes end the route. Gausium lists 5° of gradeability and obstacle detection down to 20 mm on the Phantàs (manufacturer specification). A 30 mm threshold plate, a lift lip or a cable across a doorway is not something the machine climbs; it is where the route stops. Neither model takes stairs, so a four-level building needs a charger on every level or a person to move the machine between them, and that person becomes part of the nightly routine whether anyone planned for it or not.

Name what stays with people before the trial, because it is the part buyers underestimate: the strip beside a wall that furniture hides, door reveals, bathroom floors, spills, and anything the scrub deck physically cannot overlap. A 330 mm deck down a 2.4 m corridor still leaves a strip at each wall for a person to finish.

Test three: will anyone supervise it at night

A cleaning robot is not unattended equipment. It is equipment with a short daily service routine and a fault path that needs a human. The Phantàs carries 11.5 L of clean water and 10.5 L of waste. The C40-P1 carries 16 L clean and 11 L waste on Keenon's own page, while several resellers list 14 L of waste water for the same model — a conflict to settle on the delivered datasheet rather than on a website.

How much floor one tank covers cannot be calculated from either sheet, because neither manufacturer publishes a solution rate in litres per 100 m². That figure only comes from a trial on your floor. Any claim about tank endurance in square metres is a claim about somebody else's building.

Dry waste is better documented. Gausium says the Phantàs's 6 L dust bag holds three to seven days of dust; Keenon says the C40-P1's 8 L bag holds four to eight days. Both machines return to the charger on their own. Neither clears a jam, resets a fault, or gets through a locked door at two in the morning, so the real question is who is in the building when it stops.

The cheapest part of this test is the one most often skipped. Somebody has to look at the floor at seven, not at the coverage report. A machine whose work nobody inspects is a machine nobody trusts, and the first morning it leaves a streak across a lobby is the morning it stops being used.

When the answer is no

Some buildings should not buy one yet. Under about 1,000 m² of mostly irregular floor, the machine tends to spend more time being moved than cleaning, which is why TASKI positions this class at areas up to 1,000 m².

Also no: a site with no secure overnight access, a floor that cannot go wet such as unsealed timber or open vinyl seams, a building whose real problem is toilets and food areas rather than large flat surfaces, and any site where nobody will own the morning check. In each of those cases the money is better spent on equipment that matches the soil, and a robot bought anyway becomes the story of why automation did not work.

What to ask for before you commit

A one-week supervised trial on your own route, with your own staff, is the only evidence that settles the first two tests. Ask for runtime in writing for the mode you intend to run, because scrubbing and sweeping are different figures on both machines, and ask what the machine does when it faults at night with nobody on site.

Ask for the delivered price for your postcode rather than the dealer figure. The published wholesale dealer prices are USD 9,250 for the Phantàs and USD 10,700 for the C40-P1 as of November 2026, both made to order on an 8–12 week lead time with a 12-month standard warranty, on-site setup and training, and Tier 1–2 support (Robotist product pages). Freight, duty and commissioning sit on top of that, and the number that matters is the one that lands.

If the overnight problem is watching the building rather than washing it, the machine you want belongs to a different category — a quadruped on a patrol route, not a scrubber.

Then write down the name of the person who checks the floor at seven, before the pallet arrives. That name decides more about whether the robot is worth it than any figure here.

title: Floor Cleaning Robot Australia: Hotels, Airports and Malls
excerpt: A hotel, an airport and a shopping centre buy three different machines. Route width, the quiet window and vertical transport decide which floor robot fits which building.
seoTitle: Floor Cleaning Robot Australia: Hotels, Airports, Malls
metaDescription: Hotels need quiet routes, airports need coverage in a short window, malls need a route around the public. How the building picks the machine.

faq.q: Which building type is easiest to automate?
faq.a: A hotel or an office with regular corridors, a real night window and a charger on each level. Airports are hardest because the quiet window is short and the floor is never empty, so coverage per hour matters more than battery endurance.

faq.q: Can a floor robot work in a shopping centre during trading hours?
faq.a: It can, where the malls are wide and the machine is quiet enough to work around people. Narrow tenancies, food-court seating and escalator approaches are better done before opening or after closing, so most centres run a mixed schedule.

faq.q: How many machines does a multi-level hotel need?
faq.a: Neither the Phantàs nor the C40-P1 climbs stairs, so the count follows the number of levels you want cleaned unattended. One machine plus a charger per level is the simplest plan; one machine and a person to move it between floors is cheaper and depends on someone being there every night.

faq.q: What is the real lead time in Australia?
faq.a: Both machines are made to order, so plan on 8–12 weeks from order to commissioning, plus freight to your postcode. Add the site assessment and the trial week in front of that, and add the consumables kit lead time behind it.

content:
A hotel, an airport and a shopping centre all set out to buy "a floor cleaning robot", and none of them is buying the same thing. The building sets the route, the route sets the machine, and the budget settles whatever is left over.

Australian buyers tend to shop by machine first: which model, what coverage, what price. The order is backwards. A 400 mm scrub deck is the right answer for a hotel lobby at two in the morning and the wrong answer for an airport concourse that has to be finished inside a three-hour window.

What each building is really buying A hotel buys silence and a tight route. An airport buys coverage per hour inside a short window. A shopping centre buys a route that survives the public still being in the building.

Hotels: silence, narrow routes, one floor at a time

A hotel's floor is two floors. The lobby is stone or tile and wants scrubbing; the guest corridors are short-pile carpet and want vacuuming. The C40-P1 detects carpet and hard floor and changes mode without being told (Keenon product page, manufacturer specification, checked November 2026), which is the reason it suits this building type better than a pure scrubber.

Width decides the corridors. Both machines need 650 mm of clear passage. The Phantàs is 585 × 445 × 619 mm and the C40-P1 is 616 × 550 × 690 mm with its squeegee fitted, against a corridor that was designed for two housekeeping carts to pass. Walk the guest floor at 11pm with a tape before you sign anything.

Silence matters more here than on any other site, because the machine runs under occupied rooms. Gausium lists a quiet mode at or below 60 dB on the Phantàs (manufacturer specification). Treat that as the manufacturer's figure for one mode and ask what the machine reads in scrub mode with the vacuum running, which is the mode a lobby actually needs.

Stairs end the argument. Neither machine climbs, so a ten-level hotel either buys a charger for each level or assigns someone to move the machine between them. The C40-P1 supports lift and door passage through the building's IoT system and the Phantàs can be integrated with lift control as a separate on-site project — both are manufacturer claims, both need the building's lift contractor involved, and neither is a feature you can assume on the day of delivery.

What stays manual in a hotel is the room itself: bathrooms, beds, turndown, the strip beside the wardrobe. The robot is a lobby-and-corridor machine, and the staffing plan should say so rather than implying a whole shift comes out of the roster.

Airports: the window sets the shift

An airport is the one site where the machine's endurance matters less than the clock, because the building never really empties. A terminal may give a cleaning crew two or three hours of low footfall, and inside that window the only number that matters is square metres per hour with people still walking through.

Gausium rates the Phantàs at 1,188 m²/h theoretical scrubbing, with a practical range of 350–700 m²/h. Keenon rates the C40-P1 at up to 1,100 m²/h at a 400 mm scrub width. On a concourse with a crowd, plan on the practical figure rather than the rated one, and plan the window at two hours rather than the three on the roster.

Endurance still shapes the shift, because a scrub charge is short. Keenon's page gives up to 5 hours scrubbing and up to 12 hours sweeping for the C40-P1, and Gausium gives 4.5 hours scrubbing and 6 hours sweeping for the Phantàs. Our own C40-P1 product page quotes 15 hours of continuous runtime; treat that as a sweeping figure, not a scrubbing one, and get the runtime for your mode in writing — it is the single most consequential number on the sheet and the one most often quoted out of context.

The answer to a short window is a spare battery. The C40-P1 swaps cells in about five seconds according to Keenon, which turns endurance into a staffing question: somebody has to own the spare, keep it charged, and know where it is at 3am. Without that, the five-second swap is a specification, not an operation.

Wet floor is the airport-specific risk, because the machine works in a crowd rather than after it. Keenon lists maximum suction of 23,500 Pa for water recovery, and both machines finish with a squeegee, but the pass leaves a damp strip for a minute or two. Time the pass around a security queue and a boarding call, not against a clock on a chart.

Shopping centres: working while the public is there

A shopping centre gives a cleaning robot two very different jobs. Before opening, it is a coverage problem: wide malls, tiled concourses, long straight runs, and a machine that can do the lot in one charge. During trading, it becomes a route problem, and the machine has to work around people who will walk in front of it, stop in front of it, and leave a pram in the way.

Food courts are where scrubbing earns its place, because the soil is grease rather than dust. The C40-P1 lets an operator set the detergent ratio in the app, and Keenon offers an automated fill-and-drain workstation for it. The Phantàs carries 11.5 L of solution and ships with a charging station, so ask whether a water station exists for the configuration you are quoted. Neither fact tells you how many square metres a tank covers — no manufacturer publishes a solution rate in litres per 100 m², so the refill rhythm is a trial result, not a datasheet number.

Vertical transport is the hard boundary. Escalators and travelators are not on the route, Gausium lists 5° of gradeability for the Phantàs, and a 30 mm threshold plate or a loose entrance mat stops the machine where a person would step over it. Count the mats on the route before you count the benefits.

After closing, the centre is a security environment. The machine needs a route that stays inside the patrolled area, a charger that is not behind a shutter, and someone who knows how to recover it if it stops in a service corridor at 1am.

What Australia adds to the decision

Both machines are made to order and imported, which sets the clock at 8–12 weeks with a 12-month standard warranty, on-site setup and training, and Tier 1–2 support (Robotist product pages, checked November 2026). The published wholesale dealer prices are USD 9,250 for the Phantàs and USD 10,700 for the C40-P1 as of November 2026 — dealer figures in US dollars, so the landed number for a Perth or Darwin postcode is a different conversation from the one for Sydney.

Spares are the part of an import nobody budgets for. Roller brushes, squeegee blades, HEPA filters and dust bags are consumables that wear at a rate set by your floor, and the question to ask before signing is the price and lead time of a consumables kit, not the price of the robot. A machine waiting three weeks for a squeegee blade is a machine that is not cleaning.

Dust load also differs by state. A dry inland summer loads a bag faster than a coastal site does, and the manufacturer's "three to seven days" for the Phantàs's 6 L bag or "four to eight days" for the C40-P1's 8 L bag is a range, not a schedule. Check the bag at the end of week one and set the routine from what you find.

Five measurements to take before you order

One: the narrowest clear doorway on the route, measured with the door open and the closer in place. Two: every level change, threshold and mat, with its height. Three: how many floors, how many lifts, and whether the machine gets its own charger on each. Four: the distance from the route to the nearest tap and drain. Five: the real quiet window in hours, taken from the building's own operations log rather than the cleaning contract.

Those five numbers decide which machine fits, and none of them appear on a product page. A site assessment that does not produce them is a sales call.

If the guest-facing problem at your property is greeting and guiding people rather than cleaning the floor, that is a different machine and a different budget — a service humanoid like the MOYA sits in that conversation, and no amount of scrub-deck width solves it.

Then book the trial, run the machine on your own route for a week, and keep the tape measure in the cab. The building was always going to decide.

title: Gausium Phantas Mapping: How the Robot Learns Your Floor
excerpt: The Phantàs maps from its dock, in one session, and every route afterwards sits on that map. Glass, black plinths and a moved dock are what it gets wrong.
seoTitle: Gausium Phantas Mapping: How the Robot Learns Your Floor
metaDescription: The Phantàs maps from its dock and misses glass and black plinths. What to settle before the mapping run, and what needs a second map.

faq.q: How long does it take to map a floor?
faq.a: Gausium publishes no duration for the Phantàs. Allow about an hour of driving for a mid-sized floor, then the same again in the app drawing virtual walls, naming zones and setting the route order. The constraint is the empty-building hour, not the software.

faq.q: Do I need a Gausium engineer on site to map it?
faq.a: No. Mapping and map editing run in the mobile app, and Gausium sells this as work site staff can do. What you do need is someone who knows which parts of the building the machine must never enter, because those decisions end up as virtual walls nobody else can second-guess later.

faq.q: Can one map cover several floors?
faq.a: No, one map per floor. When the machine is not connected to the building lift control, the task screen only offers the map of the floor the robot is standing on. Cleaning several floors unattended needs lift integration, which is an on-site installation project, or a person to move the machine.

faq.q: What happens when the layout changes?
faq.a: Small changes are edited: zones, virtual walls and no-go areas are redrawn in the app. A new partition, a refitted café or a relocated reception desk is a new map. Gausium advertises real-time map updates for temporary obstacles such as trolleys and stock, not for walls that were built over a weekend.

faq.q: Why does it refuse to clean near a glass wall?
faq.a: A LiDAR (light detection and ranging) sensor measures distance from a returned beam, and glass returns almost nothing. Gausium states that some sensors fail in a space surrounded by glass or other highly permeable material, and its deployment guide asks for a virtual wall along any real glass wall.

content:
Every route the Phantàs runs sits on a map somebody built in one session, usually the week the machine arrived. That session decides the coverage, the skipped zone and the complaint in week three.

Gausium sells the process as easy, and in one sense it is: mapping and map editing happen in the mobile app, with no specialist tools and no engineer required (Gausium Phantàs brochure, manufacturer claim). The software is easy. The decisions are not, because a floor map is not a picture of your building. It records what the robot decided was a wall, what it was told to refuse, and the order its zones run in.

A map holds three things Geometry the robot measured, refusals you drew by hand, and a route order you set. Only the first is automatic.

The mapping run, in order

Mapping starts at the charging dock. Send the build-map command and the screen asks you to confirm the machine is on the dock and facing it; tell it there is no dock and it carries on exploring by itself (Phantàs user manual, manufacturer documentation). Either way the dock becomes the point every later route is measured from, so its final position is a mapping decision, not a facilities afterthought. Permanent power, a clear approach and a spot out of the traffic lane are what Gausium's deployment guide asks for. Move the dock a month later and the map is wrong at its origin.

The floor should be as close to empty as it will ever be. The manual sets the rule plainly: anything standing at least 20 mm off the floor is either taken away or shut behind a virtual wall. A pallet parked in a corridor during mapping becomes an obstacle the robot avoids for the life of that map, long after the pallet has gone to another site.

The machine travels at up to 0.8 m/s (reseller specification for the platform), and a mapping run is slower than that, with turns and stops to look. Give a mid-sized floor an hour and give it a closed building. Mapping a busy lobby records the shoppers, not the lobby.

What it records, and what you draw by hand

The robot measures walls, doorways and open floor with a 2D LiDAR (light detection and ranging) scanner, 3D depth cameras and an RGB camera (Gausium specifications, manufacturer data). What the sensors cannot resolve, you add in the app: virtual walls, no-go zones, and the zone boundaries a task chooses from (Gausium Phantàs product page).

Gausium's newer Smart Deployment annotates walls, carpet, glass and escalators automatically and closes off no-go areas without manual editing (Gausium deployment guide, October 2026, manufacturer claim). The Phantàs runs an earlier generation of that software, and on this machine the annotations are yours to draw at the end of the run. Budget the time, with the floor plan open beside you.

Cleaning settings sit beside the map rather than inside it. Water volume, suction level, roller brush pressure and cleaning speed are preset per cleaning mode (Phantàs user manual), which means one zone can run two very different passes depending on the mode its task uses. When a lobby looks wrong at six in the morning, the map is not always the thing to change.

What the map cannot see

Glass is the first blind spot. A LiDAR measures distance from a returned beam, and a clean glass wall returns almost nothing. Gausium's own manual is blunter than most: where a space is enclosed by glass walls or other highly permeable material, some sensors will not work, and Gausium recommends against using it there (Phantàs user manual). Its deployment documentation for the same navigation stack tells installers to draw a virtual wall along any real glass wall, and to run one around an outer glass façade so the machine cannot leave the building if it loses its position (Gausium Vacuum 40 deployment guide).

Dark surfaces fail the other way. Black plinths, black skirting and very dark stone absorb the beam, and the same guide calls for virtual walls along black bases. Mirrors and polished floors bend the reading. None of this appears as an error in the app. It appears later, as a machine that stops short of a wall or drives into one.

Then there are the things the map keeps as geometry but the machine meets as obstacles. Gausium lists a 20 mm minimum detected obstacle height and 650 mm minimum passage width on the specification sheet. The manual for the S1 PRO build of the machine gives 52 cm minimum passage, a 30 mm cap on doorsills and floor protrusions, and fences or virtual walls wherever there is a fall risk. The two documents disagree on the narrowest gap. Measure your own opening, add 100 mm, and treat that as the number the route has to fit.

One map per floor, and the lift decides whether that matters

A multi-storey building is several maps. The manual is precise about the limit: when the machine is not connected to the building lift control, the task screen only offers the map of the floor the robot is standing on (Phantàs user manual). The other floors need the lift integration or a person to move the machine between levels.

Lift integration is a building project. TASKI, which sells the same machine into contract cleaning, describes elevator integration as on-site installation and a separate project (TASKI Phantàs technical data, 2024), and Gausium's deployment guide tells buyers to settle elevator requirements at the survey. Put the lift contractor in that meeting. And a 65 kg machine is not something a cleaner carries up a stairwell at the end of a shift.

When it loses its position

A machine that cannot place itself stops and waits. The Phantàs offers three ways back, and all three need a person standing next to it: align it to the dock and confirm, scan a QR marker that was placed on the map, or push it until it recognises where it is (Phantàs user manual). The manual suggests the push method first, because it needs nothing prepared in advance.

The other two depend on mapping-day work. Dock alignment needs the dock on the map, and every QR marker has to be placed and recorded before scanning works. That is the second reason the dock position is settled before the run, and the reason marker points belong on the deployment plan rather than in a conversation three months later.

The operational question is who walks to the machine at two in the morning. The alarm list gives a first fix for each fault, but somebody has to be in the building to read it. If the site is empty overnight, either a person is rostered to the machine or the alarm goes to remote monitoring. A floor robot with a lost position is a missed round, not a support ticket.

The map is also the schedule

Tasks are built by choosing the map and then the areas, and the order you click is the order they run; zones can be dragged up or down the list afterwards (Phantàs user manual). Schedules run either by quantity, with a start time and a number of cycles, or by window, with a start and an end time, repeated on the weekdays you choose.

That click order is an operational decision hiding in a setup screen. If the lobby has to be finished before the 6am service, it goes first, not wherever the finger landed. If a zone empties the clean tank halfway through, the refill belongs in the sequence too. Nobody puts the busiest floor last on purpose once they have watched a night run.

What to settle before mapping day

  • The dock's permanent position, with power and a clear approach
  • Who clears the floor, and the hour the building is genuinely empty
  • Every glass wall, mirror, black plinth and floor light, listed, so the virtual walls go in on the same visit
  • Whether the site is one floor or several, and whether lift integration is in scope
  • Where the QR markers go, if you intend to use scan-to-position
  • Who owns the re-map after a fit-out, and where the map date is written down

Gausium says the map updates in real time as the environment changes and that temporary obstacles stay off it (Phantàs brochure; deployment guide). Read that as trolleys and stock. A new partition, a refitted café or a reception desk moved three metres is permanent geometry, and the machine will keep driving around the room that used to be there until somebody re-maps.

Where a site is choosing between the two cleaning machines we carry, navigation is rarely the difference. Both map the floor and both need the annotations. The Keenon C40-P1 scrubs on a 400 mm deck against the Phantàs's 330 mm, which changes how a route fits a corridor more than any map setting will.

If the multi-floor problem is moving linen and meals rather than cleaning floor, the lift question belongs to a delivery robot instead, and our MOYA sits in that conversation. The building only wants to answer it once.

The Phantàs carries a published wholesale price of USD 9,250 in standard configuration, as of November 2026, made to order with an 8–12 week lead time, a 12-month warranty and on-site setup and training (Robotist product page). Mapping comes inside that setup, and it is the half-day that decides the next two years. A vendor who will not book it into the schedule with you in the room is telling you what happens after the invoice.

title: Keenon C40 Datasheet: The Numbers the Spec Sheet Leaves Out
excerpt: The C40 is rated at 1,100 m²/h and 15 hours. One is a multiplication and one is a sweeping figure. What the datasheet means on a real route.
seoTitle: Keenon C40 Datasheet: What the Numbers Leave Out
metaDescription: The 1,100 m²/h figure is a 400 mm deck at top speed, and 15 hours is a sweeping number. Read the Keenon C40 datasheet like a buyer.

faq.q: Is the 1,100 m²/h cleaning efficiency realistic?
faq.a: It is the 400 mm scrub deck multiplied by the 0.8 m/s maximum cleaning speed in the manual, which gives 1,152 m²/h. In a real scrubbing pass at 0.4 to 0.5 m/s, plan on 576 to 720 m²/h. The published figure is a ceiling with no overlap, turns, doorways or tank stops in it.

faq.q: How long does the C40 actually run on a charge?
faq.a: Keenon gives up to 5 hours scrubbing and up to 12 hours sweeping, and an integrator page adds 6 hours for dust mopping. The 15 hours of continuous runtime on our own product page is a sweeping figure. For any pass that uses water, plan on five hours and a spare battery.

faq.q: Does it need a water connection?
faq.a: No. It carries 16 L of clean water and 11 L of waste. Automatic fill and drain only comes with the optional workstation, which needs a supply and a drain at the dock, so that is a plumbing decision before it is a robot decision.

faq.q: Can one C40 clean several floors?
faq.a: Only with the building lift and door control integrated through the IoT (internet of things) interface. That is an on-site project with the lift contractor. Without it, the machine stays on the floor it is standing on, and a second machine or a person moving it is the alternative.

faq.q: Is it quiet enough to run near guests?
faq.a: The manual publishes 70 dB or less, which is vacuum-cleaner territory, not background noise. It suits a hotel lobby at two in the morning and not the same lobby during breakfast service. Ask for the reading in scrub mode at working speed, which is louder than the sweep.

content:
Keenon's C40 page is more complete than most. It still hands you numbers that cannot be used as written, and leaves out the numbers that decide whether the machine fits your building.

None of that is deceit. A datasheet describes a machine on a smooth floor, with a full tank and a new battery. The buyer's work is knowing which line to discount, by how much, and what to ask for instead.

Read the coverage figure as a ceiling 1,100 m²/h is a 400 mm deck at the machine's top speed. Halve it for a real building and you are close.

1,100 m²/h is a multiplication, not a measurement

Take the deck, then the speed. The C40 vacuums and scrubs on a 400 mm brush, and its manual gives a maximum cleaning speed of 0.8 m/s (C40 user manual, reported in an independent 2026 review). Multiply the two: 0.4 m × 0.8 m/s × 3,600 seconds = 1,152 m²/h. Keenon publishes 1,100. The rated figure is the machine's width times its top speed, less a few per cent, with no overlap, no turns, no doorways and no tank stop in it. That is an editorial inference from two published figures, and the arithmetic is on the page for anyone to check.

At a scrub speed a facilities team would actually accept, somewhere between 0.4 and 0.5 m/s, the same deck covers 576 to 720 m²/h. That is the number for a shift plan. Every manufacturer quotes the same way, so this is not a mark against Keenon; it is what a rated figure is.

Sweeping is the other case. With both side brushes out the machine sweeps on 560 mm, so the same arithmetic gives 1,613 m²/h at 0.8 m/s. Keenon does not publish that number. The figure they chose is the lower of the two, which suggests the 1,100 m²/h is scrub-limited and honest as a ceiling, as long as nobody plans a building on it.

Runtime, in the mode you will actually run

Keenon publishes floor scrubbing up to 5 hours and floor sweeping up to 12 hours on a 25.6 V, 50 Ah battery (Keenon product page, manufacturer specification, checked November 2026). An integrator page adds dust mopping at up to 6 hours (FieldBots C40 integration page). Our own Robotist product page carries 15 hours of continuous runtime, which is a sweeping figure, not a wet one. Treat it as a conflict and plan on five hours for anything that uses water.

Five hours at 576 to 720 m²/h is 2,880 to 3,600 m² of scrubbed floor per charge. One integrator page describes the C40 as suited to spaces up to 4,500 m². Both statements can be true at once: 4,500 m² needs a second charge, or a battery swap, which Keenon puts at five seconds.

The pack holds 1,280 Wh, which is the number that explains the runtime better than any claim on the page. Spread across a five-hour scrub from full to empty, that is an average draw of about 256 W, which is why one battery lasts a shift and why the five-second swap, rather than a bigger battery, is the answer to a floor that outruns it.

23,500 Pa is a peak, and the page says so

Keenon states maximum suction of 23,500 Pa and notes that it is adjustable. A peak number is measured with the air path wide open; what matters on a floor is water recovery at travel speed, because that is what the 30-second drying claim rests on. Keenon presents the drying as a product of its triple-brush layout: two front rollers sweep dry waste into the 8 L bag, and a single rear roller washes behind them, so a scrubbing pass does not turn dust into mud (Keenon product page, manufacturer claim).

Test it the way you would test a mop. Run the machine across a tiled lobby at the speed your crew will accept, then walk the pass in socks two minutes later. A damp seam at the squeegee edge is normal. A wet strip that reaches the lift lobby is a scheduling problem, not a specification problem.

The tank number two sources disagree on

Keenon lists 16 L of clean water and 11 L of waste. Two independent listings, one from FieldBots and one from the ipros catalogue, give the waste tank as 14 L (ipros listing). One of them is describing a different build or rounding a figure, and from the outside there is no way to tell which. Read the label on the delivered unit and write the volume into the handover document.

The more useful number is one nobody publishes: litres per 100 m². Without a solution rate, no tank volume converts into square metres per fill, and neither Keenon nor Gausium publishes one. The first week on site answers it. The C40's designed answer is the workstation, with automatic fill and drain and the detergent ratio set in the app (Keenon product page), which is a plumbing decision at the dock rather than a robot decision.

The numbers that are not on the page at all

The product page gives minimum passable width, 650 mm. The manual gives five more, and each one can end a route: minimum passage height 75 cm, minimum turning width 80 cm, maximum obstacle height 15 mm, maximum gap width 35 mm, and a non-cleaning gradient under 8° (C40 user manual, via the independent review). A 20 mm threshold plate or a 45 mm entrance mat is outside that obstacle figure, which is how a planned route becomes a nightly detour.

Two absences matter as much. Noise is not on the product page; the manual publishes 70 dB or less, which is vacuum-cleaner territory and rules the machine out of a hotel lobby during breakfast service. And there is no manufacturer-published IP (ingress protection) rating for the C40, so it is not a machine to hose down or run on a wet dock. If a supplier calls it washdown-rated, ask for the rating document rather than the brochure.
