1,100 m²/h400 mm deck × 0.8 m/s top speed576–720 m²/h in a scrub pass
5 h scrub / 12 h sweepBattery endurance by mode5 h for anything using water
23,500 PaPeak suction, adjustableA dry seam, timed on your own floor
16 L / 11 L tanksClean and waste (11 L disputed)m² per fill unknown until week one
70 kgIncluding the batteryNot carried between floors

What it is good at, and who should not buy it

The dry and wet separation is the part worth paying for. Dry waste goes into an 8 L bag quoted at four to eight days of dust, the floor is wetted afterwards, and the two streams never meet. Carpet and hard floor are detected automatically rather than switched by hand, and a stopped task resumes at the point it stopped (Keenon product page; integrator pages). For a building that mixes a stone lobby with short-pile corridors, that is the job done in one night by one machine.

The limits are as specific. Short-pile carpet up to 10 mm, no thick pile, no uneven ground. 650 mm of clear passage, which rules out a guest corridor with two housekeeping carts in it. 70 kg including the battery, so nobody carries it upstairs. And lift or door passage needs the building's IoT (internet of things) system integrated, which is a contractor conversation before it is a setting in the app.

A site with one large tiled hall and no mats may not need this deck width at all. The Gausium Phantàs scrubs on 330 mm, fits tighter routes, and publishes a quiet mode at or below 60 dB, which matters when the space is occupied. That is the honest trade: reach against route tolerance.

If the night shift also needs a security round, a floor robot is not the purchase. That is a patrol machine with its own payload, sensors and weather limits, and a quadruped such as the MagicLab MagicDog Y1 is a separate conversation with a separate budget.

The C40-P1 carries a published wholesale price of USD 10,700 in standard configuration, as of November 2026, made to order with an 8–12 week lead time, a 12-month warranty, Tier 1–2 support and on-site setup and training (Robotist product page). Before signing, ask for four things in writing: runtime in scrub mode, waste tank volume on the delivered unit, the noise figure at working speed, and the passage height of your narrowest doorway. None of those are unreasonable questions, and the answers are the difference between a datasheet and a plan.

title: Robots That Clean: Where the Machine Stops and People Start
excerpt: A cleaning robot covers the floor that fits its deck, its obstacle limit and its tank. Those three numbers decide which work stays human, and they are published.
seoTitle: Robots That Clean: Where the Machine Stops and People Start
metaDescription: Cleaning robots cover open floor and stop at deck width, obstacle height and tank size. The three numbers that decide which work stays with your team.

faq.q: What can a cleaning robot not do?
faq.a: It cannot reach into inside corners, behind door leaves, around column bases, under shelving or up a skirting line, because its deck is a rectangle that has to travel. It cannot decide what a spill is, only drive around it or stop. And it cannot judge whether a floor is clean, which is the part of the job the client is paying for.

faq.q: How much floor does one charge cover?
faq.a: Plan on the practical figure, not the rated one. Gausium rates the Phantàs at 1,188 m²/h scrubbing and publishes a practical efficiency of 350-700 m²/h. At 4.5 hours of scrubbing that is 1,575-3,150 m² per battery. A shift plan built on the rated number is short by half.

faq.q: Does the machine need emptying during a shift?
faq.a: The wet tank does. Neither manufacturer publishes litres per 100 square metres, so the square metres per fill cannot be calculated from a datasheet. Put a drain or a mop sink within a couple of minutes of the furthest zone, and roster a person to meet the machine there rather than waiting for it to stop.

faq.q: Why does the robot drive around a spill instead of cleaning it?
faq.a: Its sensors classify a spill as an obstacle. LiDAR, depth cameras, line lasers and ultrasonics measure distance; they do not identify what the liquid is or decide how to treat it. The machine avoids the patch or stops, and a person clears it. That response is a rostering decision, not a software setting.

faq.q: Is the coverage report proof the floor is clean?
faq.a: No. It proves the mapped route ran. Cleanliness is judged by someone walking the floor against an agreed standard, which is why the inspection stays human. Use the report to prove the round happened, then inspect separately, at a fixed time, against a written standard.

content:
A cleaning robot does not clean a building. It cleans the part of the building that fits its deck, its obstacle limit and its battery, and it cleans that part the same way every night. Knowing where those limits fall is most of the buying decision, because everything outside them stays a person's job.

We sell two machines that do this work: the Gausium Phantàs for lobbies, corridors and open concourse, and the Keenon C40-P1 where one unit has to sweep and scrub a mixed floor. Their published numbers answer the question a facilities manager actually asks during a trial - what will this leave for my team - more precisely than any headline coverage figure.

Three numbers draw the line Deck width, obstacle height, tank volume. Everything those three limits cannot reach is human work, and it stays human work after the invoice.

The deck is narrower than the machine

The Phantàs scrubs on a 330 mm deck, sweeps and vacuums on a 465 mm deck, inside a body 445 mm wide (Gausium specifications, manufacturer data). The C40-P1 scrubs on 400 mm and sweeps on 560 mm with two side brushes, inside a body 500 mm wide without its squeegee (Keenon product page, manufacturer data).

That difference is the arithmetic of a route. A 2.4 m corridor needs eight passes on the 330 mm deck and six on the 400 mm one before overlap (editorial arithmetic, 2,400 ÷ 330 = 7.3, 2,400 ÷ 400 = 6.0). Overlap is not optional on a wet floor, so add a pass in practice. Deck width decides how long a round takes, and the round is what a night shift is planned around.

What the deck cannot enter is what stays with your team, and no coverage figure includes it: inside corners, the strip behind a door leaf, the ring around a column base, under shelving, the skirting line, toilet pans and basins, glass, stainless steel. Gausium publishes 0 mm edge cleaning for the Phantàs, which means the deck can sit flush to a wall on its own side. It does not mean the room's corners are finished.

What the machine treats as floor

Obstacle thresholds are the second line, and they are published. The Phantàs detects obstacles from 20 mm up (Gausium specification). The C40-P1 clears a maximum obstacle of 15 mm, a maximum gap of 35 mm, a gradient under 8 degrees and short-pile carpet up to 10 mm, with a 75 cm minimum passage height and an 80 cm turning width (C40 review quoting the user manual, independent).

Read those as the machine's definition of floor. A cable cover 12 mm high is floor. A mat edge taped down is floor. A 30 mm threshold plate is an obstacle the C40-P1 climbs and the Phantàs may refuse. The report afterwards will not tell you which happened: the machine drives over it, avoids it, or stops, and the route diagram shows where it went.

The human work this creates is building maintenance, not cleaning: cable management, mat fixing, threshold ramps, and a decision about the two or three places where the floor changes level. That is an afternoon with a tape measure before the trial and a line item afterwards.

Where the water runs out

The Phantàs carries 11.5 L of clean water and 10.5 L of waste, plus a 6 L dust bag that Gausium says holds three to seven days of dry waste. The C40-P1 carries 16 L clean and 11 L waste, with an 8 L dust bag holding four to eight days (manufacturer data; an integrator listing gives 14 L waste for the same machine, so read the label on the delivered unit - recorded here as a conflict).

Neither manufacturer publishes litres per 100 square metres, so square metres per fill cannot be calculated from a datasheet, and anyone who quotes it is estimating. What you can do is make the refill a planned stop instead of an interruption: a floor drain or mop sink within a couple of minutes of the furthest zone, and a person rostered to meet the machine there.

Dry waste is the easier half. Four to eight days of dust bag on the C40-P1 makes the bag a weekly task, while wet work needs attention every shift. Plan the roster around the wet tank, not the bag.

Two machines, two shift shapes

Endurance by mode is where the two machines separate, and it changes the roster more than the coverage figure does. Gausium publishes 4.5 hours scrubbing, 6 hours sweeping and 10 hours dust mopping for the Phantàs, with about two hours to charge and a quiet mode at or below 60 dB (manufacturer specification). Keenon publishes up to 5 hours scrubbing and up to 12 hours sweeping for the C40-P1, a two-hour charge, and a five-second battery swap on a 1,280 Wh pack (25.6 V, 50 Ah).

In practice: a dry sweeping round in a large shed suits the C40-P1, whose 12 hours and fast swap mean the machine barely stops. A hotel lobby with guests at 9pm suits the Phantàs, which runs quieter and scrubs for 4.5 hours - enough for one evening round, not enough for a double shift without a charge window.

BuildingWhat the shift looks like
Hotel lobby and corridorsOne 4.5 hour scrub round between 10pm and 3am, quiet mode, one charge; edges and room interiors by hand
Airport or mall concourseTwo rounds with a battery swap in the middle; spill response stays staffed all night
Warehouse or distribution floorDry sweep on 12 hours, dust bag changed weekly, cable and pallet gaps mapped out of the route

The spill is the test

The C40-P1 carries ten detection components - LiDAR, two stereo cameras, four line lasers and three ultrasonic modules (Keenon product page). The Phantàs uses LiDAR and 3D depth cameras. Both see a spill as an obstacle, which is the honest description: the machine drives around the puddle or stops short of it, and neither behaviour is cleaning.

Keenon publishes a 30-second drying time after scrubbing (manufacturer claim, with no stated condition for floor type, airflow or water volume). Treat it as a ceiling, not a promise, and keep the wet-floor sign with the person, because the machine cannot judge whether a lobby is safe to walk on at six in the morning.

That makes spill response a rostering question: who attends, how fast, and whether anyone is awake in the building at 2am. A robot stopped in a corridor is not a machine failure; it is a decision nobody made on the roster.

The inspection is the product

A coverage report proves the route ran. It does not prove the floor is clean, and the gap between those two statements is where most disappointments live. The numbers make it concrete. Gausium rates the Phantàs at 1,188 m²/h scrubbing and then publishes a practical efficiency of 350-700 m²/h - a factor of 1.7 to 3.4 between the sheet and the floor.

Keenon's 1,100 m²/h is the product of the 400 mm deck and the 0.8 m/s maximum cleaning speed: 400 mm × 0.8 m/s × 3,600 s = 1,152 m²/h, so the published figure multiplies two maxima together (editorial arithmetic from Keenon's own manual figures). At a scrub speed of 0.4-0.5 m/s the same deck covers 576-720 m²/h. Those are the numbers to put in front of whoever approves the headcount: a plan built on 1,188 m²/h will be short by half, and a plan built on 400 m²/h will be met.

What to write down before the trial

  • The narrowest opening on the route, measured rather than estimated
  • Every mat, cable cover, threshold plate and gully, with its height
  • The number of inside corners and column bases the deck cannot enter
  • The nearest drain or mop sink to the furthest zone
  • Who inspects the floor each morning, and against what written standard
  • What the hours the machine frees will be used for

That list is also the trial's script. Run the machine for a week with those numbers on paper and the split between machine work and human work becomes visible, with times attached. Without it, the trial produces an opinion.

Both machines carry published wholesale prices in standard configuration, as of November 2026: the Gausium Phantàs at USD 9,250 and the Keenon C40-P1 at USD 10,700. Both are made to order on an 8-12 week lead time with a 12-month warranty, and on-site setup and training are part of the deployment.

Send us the floor plan and the shift roster. We will tell you which parts of the building the machine should never be asked to clean.

title: Humanoid Robot Research: Six Projects One Machine Can Carry
excerpt: A humanoid in a lab is an instrument, and its joint count, battery swap and control API decide which papers it can carry. Six projects, and the number that constrains each.
seoTitle: Humanoid Robot Research: Six Projects One Machine Can Carry
metaDescription: Six research projects one humanoid can carry, and the joint count, battery routine and control API that decide whether a lab gets publishable data.

faq.q: How many degrees of freedom does a research humanoid need?
faq.a: Count the joints the project touches, not the headline number. The LimX OLI has 31 active body joints - 6 per leg, 7 per arm, 3 in the waist and 2 in the neck - and the two standard grippers add one joint each, which is where a 33-DOF figure comes from. Five-finger hands are an option, not the standard build.

faq.q: Can a lab run a humanoid on one battery?
faq.a: Not for a full session. LimX publishes about 1.5 hours per 9,500 mAh pack on the specification sheet and about two hours in its FAQ from laboratory testing. A three-hour experiment is two to three packs, and each swap is a seated procedure with the robot powered down. Budget a second battery in the grant.

faq.q: Does the platform ship with a simulation model?
faq.a: The OLI ships with a complete URDF and support for Isaac Sim, MuJoCo and Gazebo, so a lab can train and test before the machine arrives. With an 8-12 week lead time on a made-to-order unit, that is a semester's worth of simulation work available before delivery, and it is the cheapest reason to choose a platform that publishes its model.

faq.q: What breaks first in a student lab?
faq.a: Position calibration and wear parts. LimX recommends joint zero calibration after a period of use or an accidental fall, and the 12-month warranty excludes wear parts and consumables. A fall costs a calibration cycle, not a repair, but a damaged joint module on a made-to-order machine can idle a project for weeks, so spares belong in the original order.

faq.q: Which platform suits manipulation research?
faq.a: One with dexterous hands and a published payload per arm. The OLI carries 3 kg per arm, and LimX notes that this varies with pose and extension. PNDbotics fits five-finger hands with six finger joints to the ADAM SP, which is the configuration to specify when the study uses real objects rather than blocks.

content:
A humanoid in a laboratory is an instrument, and an instrument is judged by the questions it lets you ask. That makes the buying decision unusually literal: the joint count, the battery routine and the control interface decide which experiments are possible, and which ones quietly are not.

Two platforms carry most research work we sell into: the LimX OLI, a 165 cm bipedal machine with an open SDK and a published simulation model, and the PNDbotics ADAM SP, a 1.67 m platform built around five-finger hands. Both are made to order, both arrive in 8-12 weeks, and both are specified by numbers a lab can check before it commits a grant.

Read the joint count first A body joint and a gripper joint are not the same resource. The project list comes after that distinction, not before it.

Read the joint count before the project list

LimX publishes 31 active degrees of freedom in the OLI's body: six per leg, seven per arm, three in the waist and two in the neck (LimX OLI specification, manufacturer data). The 33-DOF figure on our own product page is that 31 plus the two 1-DoF grippers fitted as standard (editorial arithmetic, 31 + 2). Fit the optional 6-DoF five-finger hands and the total changes again.

That matters because the numbers answer different questions. Leg joints are the locomotion resource: 6 per leg gives a knee, a three-axis hip and a two-axis ankle, which is the minimum for gait work with lateral weight shift. Arm joints are 7 each, enough for a wrist that can orient a tool. Hand joints are the manipulation resource, and a 1-DoF parallel gripper will not hold a study about in-hand reorientation no matter how many body joints sit behind it.

PNDbotics takes the other route: 41 degrees of freedom in the ADAM SP, with six per leg, thirteen per arm once the six finger joints are counted, and three in the waist (PNDbotics wiki, manufacturer data). The per-limb rows sum to 35 before the head, against a published total of 41, so ask the vendor to reconcile the allocation before you write hand degrees of freedom into a specification. It is a fair question, and the answer changes what the arm can be asked to do.

The API is the platform

A humanoid a lab cannot program is a demonstration. On the OLI, LimX publishes a modular SDK with end-to-end Python, low-level APIs for joint and end-effector control, high-level APIs for walking, mobile manipulation, stationary manipulation and teleoperation, plus sensor APIs for vision and IMU data (LimX OLI FAQ, manufacturer documentation).

Just as important, it ships a complete URDF with support for Isaac Sim, MuJoCo and Gazebo. A platform without a usable simulation model costs a semester before the first experiment, and with an 8-12 week lead time that semester is otherwise spent waiting. Train the policy in simulation while the machine is on the water, then spend the delivery week on sim-to-real, not on setup (editorial inference from the published lead time and the published model support).

Compute is split, which suits research. Motion runs on a Rockchip RK3588 with 8 GB of RAM and 64 GB of storage; perception runs on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX rated at 157 TOPS with 16 GB and 1 TB (LimX specification). Perception work therefore does not compete with the balance controller for cycles, and a vision model can be deployed on the robot rather than beside it.

One and a half hours, or two

The battery is the hard constraint on any experiment design, and here the manufacturer publishes two figures. The specification sheet gives about 1.5 hours per 9,500 mAh slide-out pack; the FAQ gives approximately two hours, from laboratory testing, with runtime varying by mode, workload and environment (spec, FAQ). Recorded as a conflict: plan on the shorter figure and treat the longer one as a best case.

Charging is 58.8 V at 10 A, and the pack is designed to be swapped rather than waited on. The procedure LimX publishes is done with the robot seated: power off, remove the pack, insert a charged one, press the power button briefly then hold it for two seconds, wait for the chest LED to show zero-torque mode, enter damping mode, then stand. LimX asks for at least 1 m of clearance during the sit-to-stand transition. That is a five-minute procedure with two people, not a hot swap mid-experiment.

So a three-hour session is two to three packs (editorial arithmetic, 3 h ÷ 1.5 h), and a second battery is part of the instrument, not an accessory. A lab that orders one pack has a 90-minute experiment, which is enough for a demonstration and not enough for a dataset.

Three kilograms per arm, and what the hands add

LimX publishes a maximum load of 3 kg per arm for the OLI, with actual capacity varying by pose and extension, and a maximum joint torque of 150 N·m on the highest-torque motor in the set (LimX specification, manufacturer data with the footnote attached). Three kilograms at full extension is a fraction of that; the useful way to read the figure is as a limit on the object, not on the gesture.

The hand options decide manipulation work. Standard is a 1-DoF parallel gripper and a humanoid hand; the 6-DoF five-finger hand is optional. The hand mounts expose 24 V power and RS485 communication so third-party hands - LimX names BrainCo's second-generation hand and INSPIRE's two-finger gripper - can be fitted without rewiring the arm.

The ADAM SP is specified around that problem: five-finger hands with six joints per hand, 62 kg total, a top walking speed of 1.5 m/s, a 1,172 Wh pack (46.2 V, 25 A), knee and hip torque around 340 N·m and arm torque around 60 N·m, with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX 16 GB for perception and an Intel NUC12WSKi7 for motion (PNDbotics wiki, manufacturer data). One honest note from the same source: the SP's head is listed for display, with articulated neck joints appearing on the Pro model. Human-robot interaction studies that need gaze should account for that.

Six projects, and the number that constrains each

ProjectWhat constrains it
Gait and balanceSix leg joints and a low-level joint API; simulation model for pre-training
Manipulation with real objectsHand joints and 3 kg per arm, less at extension
Human-robot interactionA neck with joints, voice interaction, a 1 m safety envelope
Teleoperation and datasetsSensor APIs with timestamps, a control path fast enough to demonstrate with
Teaching a cohortCalibration routine, repairable joints, spares on the shelf
Public demonstrationThe action library and OTA updates - 15+ preset actions on the OLI

The teaching row is the one labs underestimate. LimX recommends joint zero calibration after a period of use or an accidental fall, run from the controller, and publishes a maintenance routine of dust removal and screw checks. That is a good sign - the procedure exists and students can run it - but it also means a fall costs a calibration cycle, and a term with forty students will produce falls.

What breaks in a student lab

Start with the mass. A 55 kg machine at 165 cm and a 62 kg machine at 167 cm are not bench instruments: they need floor space, a clear operating area, and the discipline of keeping 1 m of clearance, which is what LimX asks for during operation and recovery. On the OLI, LimX lists a handheld emergency stop as an option, and separately documents pressing both joysticks to cut power to the joints, plus a damping mode that lets the machine fall slowly instead of dropping.

Then the parts. The 12-month warranty excludes wear parts and consumables, and a made-to-order machine has an 8-12 week lead time, so a replacement module ordered after a failure costs a term. Order the spares with the robot: a spare battery, a spare gripper, and whatever joint module the vendor will sell you. LimX also supports remote log analysis and on-site repair for major faults under contract, which is worth confirming in writing before the purchase order, because a lab on a semester timetable cannot wait for a shipping cycle.

The last constraint is supervisory. A humanoid that walks is a machine that can fall in front of people, and the safe pattern is the one the manufacturer prints: an open area, the robot in sight, a person with the emergency stop, and no experiment that requires the robot to work near an untrained visitor.

What to do next

Write the experiment first, in one page: the joint the study moves, the object it manipulates, the duration of a session, and the data it logs. Then match it to a platform. If the answer is locomotion or sim-to-real work, the LimX OLI at a published wholesale price of USD 65,900 in standard configuration, as of November 2026, is the straightforward fit. If it is dexterous manipulation with real objects, the PNDbotics ADAM SP at USD 89,000, as of November 2026, carries the hands and the torque.

Both carry a 12-month warranty, ship made to order in 8-12 weeks, and arrive with on-site setup and training. Ask for the URDF, the SDK documentation and the maintenance schedule before you sign, and ask which joint modules can be replaced by your own technician. A lab that can service its own robot runs more experiments per year than one that waits for a technician.

Tell us the paper you are trying to write and the session length you need. We will tell you which platform gives you the data for it, and which spares to order with it.

title: Human Robot Interaction Research: Design the Study First
excerpt: Interaction studies fail on protocol, environment and logging before they fail on hardware. Here is what a platform has to expose, and the four numbers that decide the session.
seoTitle: Human Robot Interaction Research: Design the Study First
metaDescription: What a humanoid must log, how long a session actually runs, and which measures decide the platform. A study-design guide for HRI labs.

faq.q: How many degrees of freedom does an HRI study actually need?
faq.a: Count the joints your measures touch. The Fourier GR-3 is quoted as 55 degrees of freedom, but that figure includes two optional 12-DOF hands. The body carries 31: two in the neck, seven per arm, three in the waist and six per leg. A study of approach, posture and gaze uses the 31 and never moves the other 24.

faq.q: How long can one session run on a battery?
faq.a: Shorter than the runtime figure suggests. Fourier publishes approximately 3 hours for the GR-3 from a 936 Wh pack, which works out to 312 W of average draw. The robot is rated at roughly 936 W. A protocol that keeps it walking and gesturing draws several times the average, so plan the session around a logged battery swap rather than a three-hour block.

faq.q: Which questionnaire should the protocol use?
faq.a: Two are common and they measure different things. The Godspeed series has 24 items across five subscales: anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, perceived intelligence and perceived safety. The RoSAS has 18 items across three factors: warmth, competence and discomfort. Pick before you shortlist hardware, because discomfort scores are only meaningful if the study also logged distance and speed.

faq.q: Does ISO 13482 cover a university study?
faq.a: It gives you a hazard framework, not a test. ISO 13482:2014 covers personal care robots through hazard identification, risk assessment and intended-use scenarios. It does not set limits, test methods or enforcement. A revision covering service robots with functional-safety guidance is in final approval. Until it lands, your protocol writes its own speed limit and stop procedure.

faq.q: What has to be in the participant information sheet?
faq.a: What the robot records, in what form, for how long, and what withdrawal does to the recording. Australia's National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research 2025, in force since 23 June 2026, requires consent that is voluntary, informed and understandable. If the platform cannot export or delete one session's log, you cannot honestly promise deletion.

content:
Interaction studies fail on protocol, environment and logging long before they fail on hardware. The robot is usually the most reliable part of the experiment. What breaks is the study around it: a measure chosen after the purchase, a session that outruns the battery, and a log nobody can align to the video.

That ordering has a practical consequence for a lab buying a platform. The protocol, the measures and the consent documents decide which machine you need, not the other way round. This is what to settle first, and what to ask a vendor before the ethics submission rather than after it.

Three documents before the shortlist The protocol, the measure set and the participant information sheet. The hardware requirement falls out of those three, and so does most of the risk in the budget.

The 55-joint headline is 31 joints in the body

Fourier quotes 55 degrees of freedom for the GR-3 (Fourier GR-3 documentation, manufacturer specification). The number is real, and it is also a maximum configuration. Break it down from the same document: two joints in the neck, seven per arm, three in the waist, six per leg. That is 31 body joints. Add two optional 12-DOF dexterous hands and you reach 55. With the standard 6-DOF hands the machine is a 43-joint build (editorial arithmetic; Fourier's own joint table lists exactly 31 body joints, numbered 1 to 31).

For an interaction lab this matters more than it sounds. If your dependent variables are approach distance, posture, response latency and rated likeability, the 24 hand joints are inventory you paid for and never move. If your work is handover, gesture or tool use, the hands are the experiment and the body is the carriage.

Study elementWhat the platform has to exposeEvidence class
Proxemics and approachCommanded versus actual velocity, distance to participantRobotist observation
Gaze and attentionHead joint angles with timestamps; 2 DOF in the GR-3 neckManufacturer specification
DiscomfortLogged distance and speed, not only questionnaire scoresEditorial inference
Trust after failureError states surfaced as data, not as a lightRobotist observation
Longitudinal exposureRuntime per charge, swap time, behaviour stability across weeksManufacturer specification

A session is as long as the battery, not as long as the protocol

The GR-3 carries a 936 Wh pack, split as 702 Wh plus 234 Wh, weighing 5.1 kg together, and Fourier publishes roughly 3 hours of runtime and 1.5 hours to charge (manufacturer specification). Divide one by the other: 936 Wh over 3 hours is 312 W of average draw. The same document gives the robot a rated power of about 936 W. At rated power the pack lasts one hour (editorial arithmetic, both figures from Fourier's specification table).

No study runs a humanoid at rated power for three hours, and no study runs it at average draw either. The honest reading is that runtime is a function of what the protocol asks the body to do, and the published figure describes a low-motion session. A study of expressive gesture, walking approach or repeated handover sits somewhere between the two numbers, and the only way to know where is to measure it in the pilot.

That makes the battery swap a protocol event rather than maintenance. Both packs are hot-swappable, so the machine does not need a cold start, but a swap still interrupts the session, changes who is in the room and adds a minute of unexplained activity for the participant. Log it as an event with a timestamp, the same way you log a trial boundary. Where continuous operation matters more than mobility, a tethered supply removes the variable entirely — worth asking about, rarely offered as standard.

What the robot records, and what you have to instrument

Read the sensor list as a data sheet, not a feature list. The GR-3 documents a monocular camera, a 6-axis IMU, a 360-degree microphone array, tactile sensors on the head and torso, and a speaker rated up to 15 W. Compute is an AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS with 32 GB and a 1 TB board running Ubuntu 22.04, with Ethernet, Wi-Fi 6, USB 3.0 and RJ45 (manufacturer specification).

Two things follow. First, there is no stereo or depth camera in that list, so anything about distance has to come from a source you add or from the robot's own state, and you should confirm which before writing the method section. Second, the interfaces are ordinary: Ethernet, USB and ROS-adjacent Ubuntu means a lab can attach its own cameras and record them on the same clock. A platform that only offers a tablet app and a cloud dashboard cannot give you that.

So the question to put to a vendor is narrow and answerable: can I subscribe to joint state and sensor streams at a fixed rate, with timestamps from one clock, and export a whole session as a file I can read offline? On a ROS 2 platform the answer is a recording bag. On a closed appliance it is often no, and the study then depends on a researcher holding a stopwatch next to a video that drifts out of alignment within minutes.

Consent is a design constraint, not a form

Australia's National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research 2025 has been in force since 23 June 2026, and institutions must apply the 2025 version (NHMRC). Chapter 2.2 sets the general requirements: consent must be voluntary, informed and understandable. Chapter 4.5 addresses participants whose capacity to consent fluctuates. The 2025 revision also moves review toward a risk-based model with a lower-risk pathway, which changes how much of the committee's time a well-designed study costs.

None of that is unusual. What is unusual is the object of consent. A participant is agreeing to be observed by a machine that records video, audio, range and touch, and the information sheet has to say what is held, in what form, for how long, and what withdrawal does to the recording. A robot that streams to a vendor cloud cannot support a promise of deletion, and a study that cannot delete a session has to disclose that in the sheet rather than discover it at audit.

Practical rule: test export and delete on the pilot session, not on the first real participant. If deleting a session requires a support ticket, write the retention limit into the protocol now.

Pick the measure before the machine

Two instruments carry most of the field. The Godspeed series, from Bartneck and colleagues in the International Journal of Social Robotics (2009), gives five subscales — anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, perceived intelligence and perceived safety — over 24 bipolar items on a five-point scale (Godspeed questionnaire series). The RoSAS, from Carpinella and colleagues at HRI 2017, gives 18 items across three factors: warmth, competence and discomfort.

The difference is not academic. Godspeed's animacy and anthropomorphism subscales ask participants to judge how alive and how human the machine seemed, which is a question about the body: head movement, gait, pause length, the small delays that read as thinking. The RoSAS keeps discomfort as its own factor, which is a question about the encounter: how close it came, how fast, and whether the participant could predict it.

Each choice implies hardware. Animacy work needs head and neck articulation and a face that can hold an expression — the reason care-focused machines carry a 2-DOF neck and an expression layer rather than a screen. Discomfort work needs distance and speed logged at a rate fine enough to correlate with the rating, which is the argument for a ROS 2 platform. Fixed 5-point scales also cap what a small study can detect, so treat sample size as a design decision made alongside the measure, not after the data arrives.

Where the study is about the encounter, Hall's distance bands are still the working vocabulary: intimate under 46 cm, personal from 46 cm to 1.2 m, social from 1.2 to 3.6 m (independent literature, widely reproduced in HRI work). Approach behaviour that ignores them produces discomfort scores that describe the approach rather than the robot — a confound you can design out by scripting distances and randomising order.

Write the safety section yourself

ISO 13482:2014 covers personal care robots through hazard identification, risk assessment and intended-use scenarios. According to an IEEE Spectrum interview with Jae-Seong Lee, it does not set limits, propose test methods or carry enforcement mechanisms for the hazards of the human-robot relationship (IEEE Spectrum). A revision, ISO/FDIS 13482 for service robots, is in final approval and adds functional-safety guidance. Useful, and still not a protocol.

So the numbers come from you. The GR-3 walks at 6.1 km/h, which is 1.69 m/s (manufacturer specification; conversion editorial). A participant standing at the inner edge of personal space, 46 cm away, has 0.27 seconds before contact at that speed. That single calculation tells a committee more than a paragraph of reassurance, and it sets the speed limit the study actually enforces.

Three items belong in the protocol: a maximum commanded speed during participant trials, a defined operating envelope — floor surface, lighting, obstacles, who else is in the room — and a stop a participant can execute without training. On the GR-3 the stop has to be reachable and obvious; on a platform with an optional hand-held e-stop, specify it as standard in the purchase order rather than assuming it ships.

What to do next

If the study is about the response to a body, start with the Fourier GR-3: USD 188,000 WDP as of November 2026, made to order in 8–12 weeks, with the 55-joint configuration including the 12-DOF hands. If it is about expressive movement in public and you need runtime and stage tooling, the LimX LUNA publishes 27 active joints, 56 kg with battery and about 4 hours per charge (LimX LUNA specification, manufacturer data). If the contribution is locomotion or control and the interaction is secondary, the LimX OLI is the cheaper instrument at 33 joints and USD 79,900 WDP, ROS 2 compatible, same lead time.

Before any of those, send the protocol. The useful answer is not a quotation. It is a list of what the platform can log, what it cannot, and which of your measures will need equipment you have not budgeted. content:
The parts of a humanoid are purchasable. The joints that decide whether it walks are not on a price list, and the integration that makes them work together is the part nobody puts in the budget. That is the honest answer to the question, and it is more useful than a number.

Nobody publishes a bill of materials for a humanoid. Not Fourier, not PNDbotics, not LimX, not us. What is published is the price of a finished platform and the price of components below the joint class that a humanoid needs. Between those two sets of numbers sits the whole cost of a build, and this is how far the published data actually reaches.

What this article does not do It does not give you a total. Any total you read is someone's estimate dressed as a fact. It gives you the blocks, what is priced, and what is unknown.

What the published platform prices do tell you

Three catalogued humanoids publish both a price and a joint count (LimX OLI and Fourier GR-3 product pages, with the PNDbotics ADAM PRO page, published WDP as of November 2026). The OLI is 33 joints at USD 79,900. The ADAM PRO is 41 joints at USD 89,000. The GR-3 is 55 joints at USD 188,000. Divide price by joints and you get 2,421, 2,171 and 3,418 dollars per actuated joint (editorial arithmetic, formula exactly as written).

That spread is the first useful finding, because it is narrow. A body with 30 actuated joints lands between USD 65,130 and USD 102,540 at those rates — 30 × 2,171 and 30 × 3,418. The range is the cost of an actuated structure built to the standard of a finished product, before hands, battery, compute, tooling and integration.

The caveat matters as much as the number. A platform price includes margin, software development, calibration, warranty and support. Per-joint figures are therefore a ceiling on what the parts cost, not a parts list. A build team sourcing its own actuators will spend less per joint and pay the difference back in engineering hours.

The joint that matters is not on a price list

Off-the-shelf robotic actuators are publicly priced, and the class is clearly delimited. CubeMars publishes its full torque table: the AK80-9 V3.0 delivers 22 N·m peak from a 490 g unit at 48 V, and the AK10-9 V3.0 reaches 53 N·m peak at 442 W for 940 g (CubeMars actuator specifications). The AK80-9 V3.0 sells for USD 579.90 in the CubeMars store, as of November 2026.

Fourier's documentation gives the GR-3 a maximum joint peak torque of 440 N·m (manufacturer specification). That is 8.3 times the highest figure in the off-the-shelf series (editorial arithmetic: 440 ÷ 53). A joint at that torque is not a hobby servo scaled up. It is usually a harmonic-drive or cycloidal reducer with a frameless motor, a dual encoder and a matched servo drive, built as a unit for one machine.

No vendor publishes a price for a 440 N·m humanoid joint. That is the single largest unknown in any humanoid build, and it is unknown by design: the units are supplied under development agreements, not catalogues. If you are budgeting a build and someone offers you a per-joint price for this class, ask for the part number and the datasheet. The answer you get is the real number.

Hands are a second programme, not an accessory

The GR-3 body carries 31 joints: two in the neck, seven per arm, three in the waist and six per leg. Fit the optional 12-DOF dexterous hands and the machine reaches 55. With the standard 6-DOF hands it is a 43-joint build (editorial arithmetic; Fourier's joint table lists the 31 body joints individually).

Read that as a budget line. Two dexterous hands add 24 actuated joints, which is close to doubling the joint count of the machine, in the smallest available volume, with the tightest tolerance and the least room for a cable. Every one of those joints has to be small, back-drivable enough to feel safe, and strong enough to grip without crushing. The published GR-3 price covers both configurations' envelope, but the increment between a 43-joint and a 55-joint machine is not separable from public data (status: unknown).

For a research group, this is where a build usually degrades first. A body can be assembled from published designs. A hand that is safe near a person, quiet, and repeatable over a thousand cycles is a project of its own, and the literature on dexterous hands is full of prototypes that never became parts.

The battery is not where the money is

The GR-3 carries 936 Wh as a 702 Wh pack plus a 234 Wh pack, 5.1 kg together, hot-swappable, about 3 hours of runtime and 1.5 hours to charge (manufacturer specification). BloombergNEF's 2025 survey puts the average lithium-ion pack price at USD 108 per kWh, with China at USD 84 (BloombergNEF battery price survey).

Multiply: 0.936 kWh × 108 = USD 101, and × 84 = USD 79 (editorial arithmetic). Those are volume prices for automotive and stationary packs, and a low-volume, certified, hot-swap robot pack costs more per kWh — but not by an order of magnitude, and not enough to change the shape of the budget. The engineering is in the connector that survives a swap under load, the battery management system, and the certification. The cells are the cheapest interesting part on the machine.

Compute is the same story. A Jetson Orin NX 16GB module is USD 999 at thousand-unit pricing and delivers 157 TOPS, the figure the LimX OLI ships with (NVIDIA Jetson pricing). The GR-3 runs an AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS with 32 GB and 1 TB of storage — mini-PC class hardware. Neither line is a budget problem. Both are integration problems.

Integration is the year nobody budgets

Every catalogued humanoid here is made to order in 8 to 12 weeks. Read that number carefully: it is the build window for a design that already exists, has already been validated, and has a supplier that has built it before. A first-time build repeats that work once per subsystem, and the subsystems do not run in parallel because they share a thermal budget and a safety case.

The GR-3 is rated at roughly 936 W and peaks at 440 N·m per joint in a 71 kg body. That combination is where build schedules die. Thermal design has to hold at continuous load. Every joint needs calibration against its own encoder pair. The control loop has to survive the frame flexing under load. And the safety case has to satisfy whoever owns the building, which is a document written by a person, not bought with a component.

Cost blockWhat decides itPublicly priced
Actuated structureJoint count and torque classOnly as a finished platform
High-torque jointsReducer, motor, encoder, drive, custom mountNo — unknown
HandsDoF per hand, grip force, cycle lifeNo — unknown
BatteryCapacity, swap mechanism, certificationCells yes, pack no
ComputeTOPS, carrier board, thermal envelopeYes
IntegrationEngineering months, test rigs, safety caseNo — it is your payroll

The team is the line item that decides the project. A humanoid build needs mechanical, electrical, firmware and controls engineers at the same time, and it needs them to stay through the integration phase, which is the least rewarding part of the work and the easiest place for a funding cycle to end. Buying does not remove engineering. It moves it: instead of building a body, the group builds behaviour and control on top of one, and the first result arrives in months rather than years.

What building actually buys you

Ownership of the mechanism. If the contribution is a new actuator, a hand topology nobody sells, or a structural approach that changes the mass budget, then building is the research and buying would remove it. That is a real category, and it is smaller than the number of groups who start there.

For everyone else the decision is about where the result lives. A platform gives you a validated body, a documented control interface, spares with part numbers, a 12-month warranty and someone to call — and it lets you spend the grant on the question rather than on the chassis. The ADAM PRO at 41 joints and USD 89,000 WDP publishes modular actuators and an integrated motion-capture pipeline, which is the build target most groups are actually aiming at, already assembled.

One last honest limit. Every figure in this article traces to a published price or a printed formula, and the block that decides the outcome — a humanoid-class joint — has no published price at all. That is not a gap in the research. It is the state of the market, and it is why a build estimate with a confident total should be treated as a sales document. Last checked: November 2026.
